laws.title: Alcohol Limit — 0.5g/L (0.3g/L New Drivers)
laws.subtitle: DGT — Stricter for new and professional drivers
laws.fullDescription: Spain: 0.5g/L BAC general limit. New drivers (first 2 years) and professional drivers: 0.3g/L. Police conduct widespread breathalyser checkpoints (controles preventivos).
laws.penalty: 0.5–1.2g/L: €500 fine, 4–6 points off licence. Above 1.2g/L: criminal offence, up to 6 months imprisonment.
exceptions: Professional drivers: 0.3g/L
New drivers first 2 years: 0.3g/L

quiz.q: Spain's BAC limit for new drivers in their first 2 years?
quiz.explanation: New drivers in Spain (first 2 years) face a stricter 0.3g/L limit.

laws.title: Spanish Culture — Siesta, Late Meals & Two Kisses
laws.subtitle: Dinner at 10pm is normal; time is flexible
laws.fullDescription: Spain operates on a late schedule. Lunch (comida) is the main meal: 2–4pm. Dinner: 9–11pm. A siesta (post-lunch rest) is still observed in smaller cities. Greetings: two cheek kisses (women to everyone; men shake hands unless very close). 'Mañana' culture means social timings are flexible — showing up 30 minutes late to a party is normal.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — expecting punctuality in social settings will frustrate you.
exceptions: Business meetings: punctuality increasingly expected
Madrid and Barcelona are more European in pace than rural areas

quiz.q: What time is dinner typically eaten in Spain?
quiz.explanation: Dinner in Spain is typically eaten between 9–11pm — much later than most other countries.

laws.title: Barcelona's Tourist Zones — No Open Drinking or Nudity
laws.subtitle: Ordenanza de medidas para fomentar y garantizar la convivencia
laws.fullDescription: Barcelona and several Spanish cities have 'civility ordinances' banning public alcohol consumption in most streets, nudity in non-beach areas, and urinating in public. Topless sunbathing is only legal on beaches. The Balearic Islands (Ibiza, Mallorca) introduced 2020 restrictions on all-inclusive alcohol packages and pub crawls in response to 'turismo de borrachera' (drunk tourism).
laws.penalty: Drinking in street: €100–€300. Urinating in public: €200–€400. Nudity off-beach: €300–€750. Balearic party package violations: up to €600,000 for venues.
exceptions: Official fiestas and festivals with permits
Beach zones clearly designated for nudity or topless
Approved outdoor terrace drinking

quiz.q: Is drinking alcohol on Barcelona's public streets generally legal?
options: No — civility ordinances ban street drinking in most areas
quiz.explanation: Barcelona's civility ordinance bans public drinking in most streets with fines of €100–€300.

laws.title: Tourist Apartment Licences — Strict Regulation
laws.subtitle: Barcelona moratorium: no new tourist flat licences since 2014
laws.fullDescription: Barcelona has had a moratorium on new tourist apartment licences since 2014. Operating an unlicensed tourist flat (Airbnb-style) in Barcelona is illegal. Platforms must remove unlicensed listings or face fines. In 2024, Barcelona announced it would not renew existing tourist flat licences, effectively banning short-term rentals. Other Spanish cities have similar restrictions.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed tourist flat: fines up to €90,000. Platform (Airbnb) fines: €600,000+ for not removing listings.
exceptions: Licensed operators with valid permits
Hotel-style registered accommodation
Rural tourism zones

quiz.q: Since when has Barcelona had a moratorium on new tourist apartment licences?
quiz.explanation: Barcelona imposed a moratorium on new tourist flat licences in 2014 — and in 2024 announced it would not renew existing ones.

laws.title: Spanish Siesta — Quiet Hours 2pm–4pm; Noise Laws
laws.subtitle: Regional ordinances — Siesta quiet hours enforced in residential areas
laws.fullDescription: Spain observes the traditional siesta break from approximately 2pm–5pm (hours vary by region). In many municipalities, residential noise restrictions apply during these hours — power tools, loud music, and renovation works are prohibited. Night quiet hours typically run from 11pm–8am, varying by city. In Madrid and Barcelona, major cities have specific noise ordinances with substantial fines. Spanish residential communities (comunidades de propietarios) can also apply their own internal regulations.
laws.penalty: Noise during siesta/quiet hours: fine €150–€3,000 depending on city. Repeated residential noise violations: neighbourhood mediation + heavier fines.
exceptions: Commercial and industrial zones may have different rules
Emergency works
Official public events with permits
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Noise Ordinance Framework — Regional Ordinances

quiz.q: What are typical Spanish siesta quiet hours in residential areas?
quiz.explanation: Spanish siesta quiet hours are typically 2pm–5pm in residential areas — power tools and renovation work are prohibited during this time in many municipalities.

laws.title: Spain's 'Gag Law' — Insulting the Crown or Flag
laws.subtitle: Ley Orgánica 4/2015 & Penal Code Art. 490–491 — Criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Criminal Code makes it a criminal offence to insult the King, the Royal Family, or the Spanish state symbols (flag, anthem) in public. Under Articles 490–491, 'slandering or insulting' the monarchy can result in up to 2 years imprisonment. The controversial Ley Orgánica 4/2015 (nicknamed the 'Gag Law' by critics) also criminalises insulting the state, burning the national flag, or publicly humiliating the Crown. Several rap musicians and social media users have been prosecuted and imprisoned for song lyrics or tweets deemed insulting to the King, drawing widespread international criticism.
laws.penalty: Insulting the monarchy: 6 months to 2 years imprisonment. Defaming the Crown in media: up to 2 years + civil damages.
exceptions: Legitimate political satire in recognised press contexts (contested in courts)
Academic or historical commentary
laws.sourceLabel: Ley Orgánica 4/2015 — Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana (BOE)

quiz.q: Under Spain's Penal Code, what can happen to someone who publicly insults the Spanish King?
quiz.explanation: Articles 490–491 of Spain's Penal Code make insulting the monarchy a criminal offence carrying up to 2 years in prison. Several artists and social media users have been imprisoned under this law.

laws.title: Bullfighting — Legal National Heritage; Banned in Canary Islands
laws.subtitle: Ley 18/2013 — National heritage; Catalonia's 2010 ban struck down in 2016
laws.fullDescription: Bullfighting (tauromaquia) was declared a national cultural heritage by Spain's Ley 18/2013, overriding some regional bans. Catalonia had banned bullfighting in 2010 (effective 2012) but the Spanish Constitutional Court struck this down in 2016, ruling it a matter of national heritage. The Canary Islands remain the one region with a legal bullfighting ban that has not been overturned. Animal rights groups continue to protest, and opinion polls show declining support for bullfighting — particularly among younger Spaniards. Attending bullfights is entirely legal for tourists.
laws.penalty: No penalty for attending or not attending bullfights. Animal activists who disrupt a bullfight may be fined for public order offences.
exceptions: Canary Islands: bullfighting remains banned
Some municipalities have voluntarily stopped hosting corridas despite national law
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Ministry of Culture — Tauromaquia Heritage Law

quiz.q: Which Spanish region successfully banned bullfighting in 2010 but had the ban struck down by the Constitutional Court in 2016?
quiz.explanation: Catalonia banned bullfighting in 2010 (effective 2012), but Spain's Constitutional Court struck down the ban in 2016 — ruling that tauromaquia is a national cultural heritage beyond regional government authority.

laws.title: Iberian Lynx Protection — World's Most Endangered Feline Is Making a Comeback
laws.subtitle: Royal Decree 139/2011 — Iberian lynx: strictly protected; Doñana rules
laws.fullDescription: The Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) was the world's most endangered feline species — down to just 94 individuals in 2002. Spain's conservation programme (Life Lince) has brought the population back to over 1,600 as of 2024. The lynx is strictly protected under Royal Decree 139/2011 — deliberately disturbing, photographing with flash, or approaching a lynx den is a serious environmental offence. Doñana National Park (UNESCO, where lynx breed) has strict access rules: visitor numbers are capped, off-road vehicles are banned, and guided tours are the only legal way to enter most zones. Sierra de Andújar Natural Park in Andalusia is another key habitat — dawn and dusk 'lynx safaris' with licensed operators are popular.
laws.penalty: Deliberately disturbing a lynx or its den: up to 200,000 € fine. Off-road vehicle in Doñana: criminal environmental offence. Entering restricted zones: €600–3,000 fine.
exceptions: Life Lince programme biologists with Ministry for Ecological Transition permits
Licensed nature tourism operators with Doñana National Park concession
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Ministry for Ecological Transition — Iberian Lynx Recovery

quiz.q: How many Iberian lynxes existed at the species' low point around 2002, making it the world's most endangered feline?
quiz.explanation: The Iberian lynx population reached a catastrophic low of just 94 individuals around 2002 — the brink of extinction. Spain's Life Lince conservation programme has since brought the population back to over 1,600 individuals by 2024.

laws.title: 'Gag Law' (Citizens' Security Law) — Fines for Unauthorized Protests Near Parliament
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2015 security law was widely criticized; 2023 reform reduced but didn't eliminate restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Citizens' Security Law (Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana, 2015) — nicknamed the 'Gag Law' by critics — created administrative offenses (avoiding criminal courts) for: unauthorized protests near parliament or government buildings (fines up to €600,000), insulting security forces online or in person (up to €30,000), posting images of police officers without authorization, and 'passive resistance' to police orders. UN Human Rights Committee, Council of Europe, and EU institutions criticized the law for violating freedom of assembly and expression. Thousands of fines were issued, including to journalists photographing police incidents. A 2023 reform by the new coalition government reduced some penalties and removed the 'passive resistance' provision, but retained restrictions on protests near parliament.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized protest near parliament: administrative fine €30,001–€600,000. Insulting security forces: €100–€600. Posting unauthorized police images: €600–€30,000.
exceptions: Journalists with press credentials retaining some photographic rights (restored in 2023 reform)
Political parties with official march permits
Religious processions with historical precedent
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Official State Gazette — Citizens' Security Law 2015

quiz.q: What maximum fine did Spain's 2015 'Gag Law' impose for unauthorized protests near parliament?
quiz.explanation: Spain's Citizens' Security Law created administrative fines up to €600,000 for unauthorized protests near parliament or government buildings — an extraordinarily high amount that bypassed criminal courts and was widely criticized by the UN Human Rights Committee and European institutions.

laws.title: Catalan Independence Crisis — Illegal Referendum, Exile, and Amnesty Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2017 Catalan independence referendum was declared illegal; leaders jailed, later amnestied
laws.fullDescription: On October 1, 2017, Catalan regional authorities held an independence referendum that the Spanish Constitutional Court had declared illegal. Spanish national police clashed with voters. The Catalan regional president Carles Puigdemont fled to Belgium. Other separatist leaders were arrested, tried for sedition, and sentenced to up to 13 years imprisonment (2019 Supreme Court ruling). The EU Court of Justice ruled that Puigdemont had immunity as an MEP while elections were pending. The February 2024 Amnesty Law — passed by the Pedro Sánchez government with separatist parliamentary support — granted amnesty to all those involved in the independence push, including those convicted. The Constitutional Court partially challenged provisions. Spain's territorial integrity and Article 155 (direct rule over regions) remain contested political questions.
laws.penalty: Under 2019 convictions: 9–13 years for sedition + rebellion. Amnesty Law 2024: amnesty for all Catalan independence-related offenses from 2012–2023. Ongoing legal challenges to the Amnesty Law.
exceptions: Acts of serious violence outside the amnesty (terrorism charges excluded)
Financial crimes unrelated to independence push not covered
Spanish Supreme Court challenged some amnesty provisions before Constitutional Court
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Official Gazette — Catalan Amnesty Law 2024

quiz.q: What Spanish constitutional provision allows the national government to impose direct rule over an autonomous community?
options: Article 155 (direct central government rule over regions)
quiz.explanation: Spain's Article 155 allows the central government to impose direct rule over an autonomous community if it fails to comply with constitutional or legal obligations — it was invoked for the first time in October 2017 against Catalonia after the illegal independence referendum, dissolving the Catalan parliament and calling new elections.

laws.title: Catalan Independence Crisis
laws.subtitle: 2017 referendum ruled illegal; Carles Puigdemont spent years in exile
laws.fullDescription: On October 1, 2017, Catalonia held an independence referendum declared unconstitutional by Spain's Constitutional Court. Spanish police violently dispersed voters, with 1,000+ injuries documented. President Carles Puigdemont declared independence on October 27; the Spanish government invoked Article 155, suspending Catalan autonomy. Puigdemont fled to Belgium to avoid prosecution. Nine Catalan leaders received prison sentences up to 13 years for sedition. In 2024, Spain's Socialist government passed an amnesty law pardoning over 400 independence movement participants, allowing Puigdemont to return. In 2024, Puigdemont briefly returned to Barcelona before leaving again.
laws.penalty: Sedition (original charges): up to 15 years. Misuse of public funds: up to 8 years. 2024 Amnesty Law pardoned those convicted. Disobedience of Constitutional Court rulings: criminal contempt.
exceptions: Spain's Constitution permits Statute of Autonomy expansions through legal channels
2024 Amnesty Law covered acts from 2012–2023 related to independence movement
Individual expression of pro-independence views is protected free speech

quiz.q: What constitutional provision did Spain invoke to suspend Catalan autonomy after the 2017 independence declaration?
quiz.explanation: Spain's central government invoked Article 155 of the Constitution to suspend Catalan autonomy and impose direct rule following the 2017 independence declaration, a provision never previously used.

laws.title: Catalan Amnesty Law 2024
laws.subtitle: Spain's parliament passed an amnesty for 400+ Catalan independence activists as coalition price
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Amnesty Law (Ley de Amnistía), approved by the Spanish Congress in June 2024, pardoned over 400 people involved in Catalonia's 2017 independence movement — including former President Carles Puigdemont (still living in Belgium) and those convicted in the 2019 Supreme Court trials. The law was the price PM Pedro Sánchez's PSOE paid to secure the votes of Catalan independence parties (Junts per Catalunya, ERC) needed to form a government in 2023. Critics — including some Supreme Court judges — argued the amnesty violated the Constitution and equality before the law. Puigdemont briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 before leaving again when arrest conditions were unclear.
laws.penalty: Amnesty law erases criminal records and ends ongoing proceedings for covered acts. Spanish Supreme Court initially resisted applying the amnesty to some charges. EU-level arrest warrants were withdrawn by Spain.
exceptions: Terrorism charges are not covered by the amnesty — some judges attempted to apply terrorism classifications to prevent pardons
The amnesty covers acts committed between 2012 and 2023
Catalan officials who committed acts in other contexts remain prosecutable
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Official State Gazette — Amnesty Law

quiz.q: Why did Spain's ruling PSOE party pass the 2024 Catalan Amnesty Law?
options: It was required by the European Court of Human Rights
It was the price to secure Catalan independence party support for forming a government
It was agreed at the Prespa-style bilateral treaty
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2024 Catalan Amnesty Law was the political price PM Sánchez's PSOE party paid to secure the parliamentary votes of Catalan independence parties (Junts per Catalunya, ERC) needed to form a government after the inconclusive 2023 election.

laws.title: Bullfighting — National Cultural Heritage vs. Animal Rights
laws.subtitle: Spain declared bullfighting national heritage in 2013, reversing Catalonia's ban in the process
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Bullfighting Protection Law (2013) declared tauromachia (bullfighting) a 'cultural heritage of special protection' — effectively overriding Catalonia's 2010 regional ban on bullfighting (the Constitutional Court struck down Catalonia's ban in 2016, ruling bullfighting was a national competence). Bullfighting generates approximately €1.6 billion annually and employs 200,000+ people. However, attendance has fallen dramatically: 1.4 million spectators in 2022 vs. 10 million in the 1990s. Younger Spaniards largely oppose bullfighting; multiple surveys show 70%+ of under-35s want it banned. The Pedro Sánchez government removed bullfighting from state broadcaster's cultural programming in 2016.
laws.penalty: Animal cruelty laws explicitly exempt bullfighting designated as cultural heritage. Unauthorized bullfights (without permits): fines. Disrupting legal bullfights: criminal prosecution under public order laws.
exceptions: Minors under 14 cannot legally attend bullfights
Some municipalities have voluntarily declared themselves 'anti-bullfighting' though this has no legal force
Bullfighting receives state subsidies that are politically contested

quiz.q: What did Spain's Constitutional Court rule regarding Catalonia's 2010 ban on bullfighting?
options: The ban was upheld as a valid regional cultural decision
The ban was struck down because bullfighting is a national cultural heritage competence
The ban was upheld only for public events, not private ones
The ban was converted into an animal welfare regulation
quiz.explanation: Spain's Constitutional Court struck down Catalonia's 2010 regional bullfighting ban in 2016, ruling that bullfighting is a national cultural heritage competence under the 2013 Protection Law — meaning regions cannot unilaterally ban it.

laws.title: Catalan Independence Referendum & Amnesty Law
laws.subtitle: Spain jailed Catalan leaders for staging an illegal 2017 independence referendum — then granted amnesty in 2024
laws.fullDescription: On October 1, 2017, Catalonia held an unauthorized independence referendum that the Spanish Constitutional Court had banned. Spanish police violently attacked voters, injuring nearly 900. Catalan leaders including former regional president Carles Puigdemont fled abroad; others were prosecuted for sedition and rebellion. Nine were convicted in 2019 with sentences up to 13 years. Puigdemont remained in exile for 7 years. In June 2024, Spain's parliament passed an amnesty law covering all those prosecuted over the independence bid — a deal facilitated by PM Sánchez needing Catalan independence parties' votes to form a government. Puigdemont briefly returned to Spain in August 2024 before fleeing again amid legal uncertainty.
laws.penalty: Before amnesty: up to 13 years for sedition/rebellion. After amnesty law (2024): charges effectively nullified for independence-related acts
exceptions: The amnesty law covers political acts but not personal enrichment crimes — some separatist financial cases continued
Spain's Supreme Court referred certain amnesty applications to the EU Court of Justice for review
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Official State Gazette – Amnesty Law 2024

quiz.q: How many years did Carles Puigdemont spend in exile after fleeing Spain following the 2017 Catalan referendum?
quiz.explanation: Carles Puigdemont fled Spain in October 2017 following the unauthorized Catalan independence referendum and spent approximately 7 years in exile (primarily in Belgium and later France) before briefly returning to Spain in August 2024 after the amnesty law passed.

laws.title: Spain's Housing Law 2023: Rent Control, Eviction Bans & Tenant Rights
laws.subtitle: Spain passed Europe's most comprehensive housing law — capping rents in stress areas and banning evictions without social housing alternatives
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley por el Derecho a la Vivienda (Housing Rights Law), signed in May 2023, was the most ambitious housing legislation in Spanish democracy. It created a register of 'stressed residential market areas' where rent increases are capped (at 3% annually for large landlords; linked to a new index for small landlords from 2025). It expanded tenant protections: mandatory extensions for vulnerable households facing eviction, requiring municipalities to provide social housing alternatives before eviction of households at risk. Large landlords (owning 5+ properties in stress areas) face stricter limits. Barcelona, Madrid, and other cities quickly applied for stressed area designation. Landlords' associations challenged the law; regional governments (especially PP-governed ones) refused to implement it.
laws.penalty: Exceeding rent caps in stress areas: fines up to €9,000. Violating eviction protections for vulnerable tenants: civil liability and procedural nullification of evictions
exceptions: Autonomous communities that don't request stressed area designation (like Madrid under PP government) are exempt
New construction is exempt from rent caps for 5 years to incentivize building
laws.sourceLabel: Spanish Official State Gazette – Housing Rights Law

quiz.q: Under Spain's 2023 Housing Law, what makes a residential area a 'stressed market' eligible for rent controls?
options: Any area where median rent exceeds €1,000/month
Areas where housing costs represent more than 30% of average household income
Any area with more than 10,000 inhabitants
Areas designated by the national government regardless of local conditions
quiz.explanation: Spain's Housing Law designates areas as 'stressed residential markets' where housing costs (rent or mortgage) represent more than 30% of average household income in the area — triggering rent caps, extended eviction protections, and other tenant rights provisions.

laws.title: Democratic Memory Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2022 law condemned Franco dictatorship and honors civil war victims
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Democratic Memory Law (Ley de Memoria Democrática, 2022) declared the Franco dictatorship (1939–1975) illegal and unconstitutional, condemned the crimes committed during the Civil War (1936–1939) and the dictatorship, removed all honorary symbols commemorating Franco and Francoism from public spaces, mandated the exhumation and identification of Civil War victims from mass graves, and banned private Francisco Franco foundations from receiving public funding. The Valley of the Fallen (Valle de los Caídos) — Franco's monumental mausoleum — was redesignated as a site of democratic memory. The law replaced the earlier 2007 Historical Memory Law and was fiercely contested by the political right.
laws.penalty: Violations of provisions removing Franco-era symbols: administrative fines; organizations that glorify Francoism can be banned
exceptions: Religious symbols that overlap with Francoist iconography present interpretation challenges
Private commemorations on private property are not directly restricted

quiz.q: How long did Francisco Franco's dictatorship rule Spain?
quiz.explanation: Francisco Franco ruled Spain from 1939 (after winning the Civil War) until his death in November 1975 — approximately 36 years, making his regime one of Europe's longest-lasting dictatorships of the 20th century.

laws.title: Bullfighting Heritage Law
laws.subtitle: Spain declared bullfighting national cultural heritage to protect it from regional bans
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Congress approved a law in 2013 declaring bullfighting (corrida de toros) an 'artistic expression' and national cultural heritage, giving it official state protection. This was a response to Catalonia banning bullfighting in 2010 (later overturned by Spain's Constitutional Court in 2016, ruling that regions cannot ban a national cultural heritage). Spain also provides public subsidies for bullfighting events. Polls show declining support among younger Spaniards — fewer than 25% support bullfighting. Animal rights organizations have increasingly challenged its status. Several cities have declared themselves 'anti-bullfighting' but cannot legally prohibit the practice.
laws.penalty: N/A — heritage law protects bullfighting from prohibition; violations of animal welfare regulations at events: fines for unauthorized cruelty beyond permitted norms
exceptions: The Canary Islands had a longstanding regional ban that pre-dated the national heritage law — its status is complex
Catalonia's 2010 ban was struck down by the Constitutional Court in 2016

quiz.q: Which Spanish region banned bullfighting in 2010, only to have the ban overturned in 2016?
quiz.explanation: Catalonia banned bullfighting in 2010 through a regional vote — the first Spanish region to do so since the Canary Islands. Spain's Constitutional Court overturned the ban in 2016, ruling that regions cannot ban a declared national cultural heritage.

laws.title: Democratic Memory Law 2022
laws.subtitle: Spain's law on historical memory expands recognition of Franco-era victims
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Democratic Memory Law (Ley de Memoria Democrática), enacted in October 2022, replaced and significantly expanded the 2007 Historical Memory Law. The 2022 law: prohibits public glorification of the Franco dictatorship and the 1936–1939 Civil War coup; mandates the removal of remaining Francoist symbols from public spaces; establishes a national DNA bank to identify the estimated 114,000 people still missing from mass graves; creates a new public prosecutor role for historical memory crimes; and establishes August 31 as a Day of Democratic Memory. The law also addresses crimes committed during the Second Republic and Republican side during the Civil War, aiming for balanced historical accounting. Critics on the right argue the law is politically motivated and opens old wounds; supporters call it essential for democratic consolidation and victim dignity. Spain is one of the last European democracies to formally address its 20th-century authoritarian past.
laws.penalty: Organizations that glorify Francoism or the Civil War coup can be denied public subsidies and face dissolution; failure to remove Francoist symbols can result in government intervention
exceptions: Religious symbols in churches may be retained if they also serve a liturgical function
Private property exempted from mandatory symbol removal
Academic and artistic treatment of the period is protected

laws.title: Catalan Independence Movement and Amnesty Law 2024
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2024 amnesty law pardoned Catalan independence figures in exchange for parliamentary support
laws.fullDescription: Catalonia's independence movement (Catalan: moviment independentista) peaked in October 2017 when the Catalan regional government held an unauthorized independence referendum (declared illegal by Spain's Constitutional Court) and unilaterally declared independence. The Spanish government invoked Article 155 of the Constitution (suspending Catalan autonomy), prosecuted leaders: former president Carles Puigdemont fled to Belgium; others were convicted of sedition and misuse of public funds in 2019 (sentences up to 13 years). In 2021, PM Pedro Sánchez pardoned the convicted leaders but did not resolve the legal status of Puigdemont. In 2024, as Sánchez needed Catalan independence party (Junts/ERC) parliamentary support to form a government, Spain enacted an Organic Law of Amnesty that effectively wiped out all criminal proceedings related to the 2017 independence events. Puigdemont returned to Spain in August 2024. The Constitutional Court upheld the amnesty law.
laws.penalty: Prior to amnesty: sedition (up to 15 years), misuse of public funds, and related offenses were prosecuted; after amnesty, all related proceedings were extinguished
exceptions: The amnesty did not cover acts involving violence or terrorism
International arrest warrants in countries that did not accept the amnesty remain potentially active
New independence-related actions remain fully prosecutable

laws.title: Canary Islands Migration Crisis and Maritime Rescue Obligations
laws.subtitle: Spain faces legal tensions between maritime rescue obligations and migration control at the Canary Islands
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Canary Islands have become the primary entry point for irregular migration to Europe from sub-Saharan West Africa — with over 39,000 arrivals in 2023 (the highest ever). Spain is legally bound by maritime law (SOLAS Convention, SAR Convention) to rescue anyone in distress at sea, and by EU asylum law to process claims from those who arrive. The Spanish Maritime Rescue Service (SASEMAR) coordinates rescues. Once on Spanish territory, migrants have the right to apply for asylum under EU law. Spain has faced tensions with the Canarian regional government demanding resources and policy changes, and with Morocco over border management. The 2015 Spanish 'hot returns' (devoluciones en caliente) — directly returning people to Morocco without asylum processing — were ruled unlawful by the European Court of Human Rights in 2020 (N.D. and N.T. v. Spain, Grand Chamber). Spain also operates the EU-funded FRONTEX operations in the Atlantic.
laws.penalty: Smugglers of migrants: up to 8 years imprisonment; employers of irregular migrants: fines up to €10,000 per worker; immigration detention: up to 60 days before release or deportation
exceptions: Asylum seekers who express fear of persecution must be processed regardless of arrival method
Unaccompanied minors have special protection status
Those in genuine medical emergency have access to treatment regardless of status

laws.title: Catalan Amnesty Law and Political Controversy
laws.subtitle: Spain passed an amnesty for independence activists to secure Sánchez's government
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Organic Law on Amnesty for acts of institutional overreach in the context of Catalan self-determination (Amnesty Law) was passed by Congress in June 2024. The law granted amnesty to hundreds of Catalan independence activists, politicians, and officials for acts related to the 2017 independence referendum and subsequent political activities. Critics, including the main opposition People's Party, argued it was unconstitutional and a quid pro quo for parliamentary support from Junts per Catalunya (Carles Puigdemont's party) needed by Prime Minister Sánchez to remain in government. Spain's Constitutional Court and the EU monitored implementation, with EU institutions divided on whether it undermined the rule of law.
laws.penalty: Acts not covered by amnesty (violence causing serious injury) remain prosecutable. Future independence referendum organizing: criminal charges for sedition or rebellion.
exceptions: Violence with serious injury explicitly excluded from amnesty
Terrorism-related acts excluded unless court determines connection to political context
laws.sourceLabel: Boletín Oficial del Estado – Ley de Amnistía

quiz.q: Why did Spain's Amnesty Law face widespread political criticism?
options: It was seen as a quid pro quo for Catalan party support enabling Sánchez to remain PM
It violated Spain's commitment to the European Arrest Warrant
It conflicted with the Maastricht Treaty on constitutional courts
quiz.explanation: Critics argued the amnesty was a political deal — Sánchez needed Junts per Catalunya's parliamentary support to remain PM, and the amnesty benefitted Catalan independence leaders including Puigdemont.

laws.title: Spain's Housing Law 2023 and Rent Cap Controversy
laws.subtitle: Spain enacted a new housing law allowing rent caps in 'stressed' markets
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Housing Law (Ley de Vivienda), passed in May 2023, was Spain's first comprehensive national housing legislation. Key provisions: it allows regional governments to declare 'stressed housing markets' where rent increases can be capped at CPI; it limits rent increases for small landlords to 3% (2024) and 2% (2025); it requires large landlords (10+ properties) to meet social housing quotas; and it creates housing policies to increase affordable supply. Catalonia and Basque Country quickly implemented rent caps. The law sparked intense debate — landlords argued it would reduce rental supply; renters groups called it insufficient. Spain's housing costs, especially in Madrid and Barcelona, have surged with tourism gentrification and limited construction.
laws.penalty: Large landlord non-compliance with social housing obligations: fines up to €900,000. Illegal eviction without proper process: civil damages and criminal harassment charges.
exceptions: New construction exempt from rent caps for 5 years to incentivize building
Tourist and seasonal rentals subject to separate regional regulations
Properties rented for under 3 years not subject to stress area caps in some regions

quiz.q: What innovative mechanism did Spain's 2023 Housing Law create for rent control?
options: A national fixed rent cap of 5% annually for all properties
Allowing regional governments to declare 'stressed markets' where rents can be capped
Requiring all landlords to register with a national housing authority
Creating a state landlord that competes with private rentals
quiz.explanation: Spain's Housing Law allows regional governments to declare 'tense residential market areas' (stressed markets) where rent increases can be capped — a flexible mechanism that lets regions with high housing costs impose controls while others don't.

laws.title: Spain's MareNostrum 5 and AI Supercomputing Hub
laws.subtitle: Spain positioned itself as a European AI and computing power hub
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) operates MareNostrum — one of Europe's most powerful supercomputers. MareNostrum 5 (launched 2023) is ranked among the world's top 20 supercomputers and is a key node in EuroHPC (European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking). Spain's government under Pedro Sánchez positioned Spain as a European AI hub — establishing the Spanish Agency for the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence (AESIA) in La Coruña (the EU's first dedicated AI supervisory authority). Spain's AI strategy includes investment in quantum computing and photonics. Spain also hosts the EuroHPC node MareNostrum and seeks to host the European AI Office's technical infrastructure.
laws.penalty: AESIA enforcement of EU AI Act: fines aligned with EU AI Act thresholds — up to €35 million for prohibited AI. Privacy violations involving AI systems: AEPD (data protection agency) fines.
exceptions: Research computing institutions have expedited access to supercomputing resources
Open source AI projects have reduced compliance burden under EU AI Act

quiz.q: What unique distinction does Spain's AESIA hold in the European Union?
options: It is the EU's largest AI research institution
It is the EU's first dedicated AI supervisory authority
It operates the EU's most powerful quantum computer
It certifies all AI products sold in the EU single market

laws.title: Spain's Democratic Memory Law
laws.subtitle: Exhumations of Franco-era victims and removal of dictatorship symbols

Historical documentation and academic study of the Franco era is protected

quiz.q: What does Spain's Democratic Memory Law require the state to do about Civil War-era victims?

laws.title: Spain's Amnesty Law for Catalan Independence Leaders
laws.subtitle: Sánchez government grants amnesty to secure investiture votes

Civil liability separate from criminal charges not necessarily extinguished

Making Catalan an official EU language

laws.title: Only Yes Means Yes and Sexual Consent Reform
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2022 sexual consent law overhauled rape and assault definitions
laws.fullDescription: Spain's 'Solo sí es sí' (Only Yes Means Yes) law, enacted in 2022, fundamentally reformed sexual offense laws by introducing an affirmative consent standard—any sexual act without explicit consent is assault regardless of whether force or intimidation was used. The law eliminated the distinction between sexual abuse and sexual assault, creating a single offense. However, the law's sentencing structure initially triggered judicial controversy when some courts reduced existing sentences, prompting an emergency amendment in 2023. The law also strengthened protections for trafficking victims and created victim support funds.

exceptions: Sentencing amendments in 2023 clarified the mandatory minimums after initial controversy
Age of consent remains 16

quiz.q: What standard did Spain's 'Only Yes Means Yes' law introduce?

laws.title: Catalan Amnesty Law and Political Crisis

laws.title: AI Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Law
laws.subtitle: Spain became the first EU country to implement a national AI regulatory sandbox
laws.fullDescription: Spain established the first dedicated national AI regulatory sandbox in the EU through the Digital Economy and Society Law (LDES, 2021) and subsequent AI regulations. The sandbox allows companies to test AI applications under regulatory supervision without full compliance obligations, enabling innovation while managing risk. Spain also implemented the EU AI Act ahead of schedule for voluntary compliance. The Spanish Agency for the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence (AESIA) was established as the national AI regulator. Spain positioned itself as an AI governance leader in the EU, with Barcelona becoming a significant AI hub. Spain's approach influenced EU AI Act implementation guidance.
laws.penalty: AI Act violations: fines up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited AI applications; high-risk AI violations: up to €15 million or 3%
exceptions: Sandbox participants operate under reduced compliance requirements during testing phase
Research and development activities have modified obligations

quiz.q: What was Spain's AESIA?
options: The Spanish Agency for the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence
quiz.explanation: AESIA (Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial) is Spain's national AI regulatory agency, established to supervise AI Act compliance — making Spain one of the first EU countries to have a dedicated AI supervisory authority.

laws.title: Spain Audiovisual Communication Law and Platform Obligations
laws.subtitle: Spain extends broadcasting rules to streaming and online video
laws.fullDescription: Spain's General Audiovisual Communication Law (2022) extended traditional broadcasting regulations to online video platforms and streaming services. The law requires platforms like Netflix, HBO, and YouTube to contribute a percentage of revenues to Spanish film and TV production, maintain Spanish and EU content quotas, and label content appropriately for age rating. The law also strengthens protections against hate speech and disinformation in audiovisual content.
laws.penalty: Fines up to 600,000 euros for minor violations; up to 1.5 million euros for serious violations; temporary service suspension
exceptions: Non-commercial video platforms
Platforms with minimal Spanish viewership
News and information services

quiz.q: What financial obligation does Spain's Audiovisual Law place on streaming platforms?
options: Pay a subscription tax to users
Contribute a percentage of revenues to Spanish film and TV production
Pay government fees for each subscriber

laws.title: Spain Coalition Government and Amnesty Law for Catalan Separatists
laws.subtitle: Spain's controversial amnesty law for Catalan independence supporters

EU pressure to resolve the conflict
A referendum of the Spanish people

laws.title: Spain Youth Housing Law
laws.subtitle: Spain mandates affordable housing for young people
laws.fullDescription: Spain enacted housing legislation creating guaranteed affordable housing options for young people under 35. The law requires regions to set aside a percentage of public housing for youth, creates social rent guarantees with rents capped at 30% of income, and establishes first-time buyer support programs. Spain faces one of Europe's most severe youth housing crises, with young people spending disproportionate income on rent and homeownership rates among youth among the lowest in the EU.

exceptions: Private market housing outside regulated zones is unaffected
Student accommodation under separate frameworks
Tourist rentals in rural areas with different rules

laws.title: Ley de Vivienda Rental Regulations
laws.subtitle: Spain's housing law with rent controls and tenant protections
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley de Vivienda (Housing Law) enables municipalities in stressed housing markets to cap rental price increases, requires large property owners to offer affordable housing in new developments, strengthens tenant protections against eviction, and taxes empty properties. In Barcelona and other declared stressed zones, rent increases are limited to CPI plus 3% for small landlords and capped at previous contract levels for large landlords. Short-term tourist rentals face increased restrictions.
laws.penalty: Landlords violating rent caps in stressed zones face fines of €9,000 to €90,000; tourist rental operation without license carries fines up to €600,000 in some regions
exceptions: New construction is exempt from rent caps for 5 years
Owner-occupied units rented for the first time have modified rules
Short-term rentals to family members exempt

Rents are capped at the previous contract level
No restrictions apply to large landlords

laws.title: Democratic Memory Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's official recognition of Franco-era victims and historical memory
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Democratic Memory Law (Ley de Memoria Democrática) replaced and expanded the 2007 Historical Memory Law. It establishes an official narrative recognizing the victims of the Franco dictatorship (1939-1975) and the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939), mandates removal of remaining Francoist symbols from public spaces, creates a state DNA bank for identifying victims, declares null and void sentences handed down by Francoist courts, and establishes a special prosecutor for crimes against humanity from the period. The law also addresses enforced disappearances.
laws.penalty: Public bodies that fail to remove Francoist symbols face administrative sanctions; falsification of historical records regarding victims carries fines; private organizations that glorify Franco face denial of public subsidies
exceptions: Museums and memorial sites may retain materials for educational purposes
Private property owners not required to remove historical elements from private spaces
Academic research and publication on the period is fully protected

Declaration of nullity of Francoist court sentences
Criminal prosecution of surviving Francoist judges

laws.title: Catalonia Amnesty Law

laws.title: Spain Tourist Accommodation Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Barcelona and other cities limiting short-term rental licenses

laws.title: Spain Valencia DANA Flood Disaster and Emergency Law Reform
laws.subtitle: Worst flooding in 50 years prompts emergency management overhaul

The disaster exposed serious failures in Spain's emergency alert system — many residents received official phone alerts only after flood waters had already struck. The government enacted emergency management law reforms requiring unified national alert standards, new dam management protocols, and a review of urban development in flood-prone riverbeds (ramblas).

laws.title: Spain Housing Emergency and Rent Control National Act
laws.subtitle: Affordable Rental and Property Speculation Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes Spain's national approach to its severe housing affordability crisis in cities like Madrid, Barcelona, and Valencia. The law creates rent control mechanisms in declared stressed rental markets, establishes a vacant property tax, mandates 30% social housing in new developments, creates homebuyer assistance programs for under-35s, and restricts Airbnb and short-term rentals in residential buildings.
laws.penalty: Fines up to 90,000 euros for landlords violating rent controls; tax penalties for vacant property owners
exceptions: Small landlords owning less than 5 properties have modified obligations
Student housing has alternative regulatory pathway

quiz.q: What age group does Spain's Housing Emergency Act create specific homebuyer assistance for?
quiz.explanation: Spain's Housing Emergency Act creates targeted homebuyer assistance programs specifically for people under 35 to address youth housing exclusion.

laws.title: Spain DANA Flash Flood Emergency and Climate Adaptation Act
laws.subtitle: Mediterranean Climate Disaster Response Law
laws.fullDescription: Responds to the devastating DANA (Dana Aislada en Niveles Altos) flash floods that killed 223 people in Valencia in October 2024, Spain's deadliest natural disaster in decades. The law creates the National Emergency Alert System with mandatory mobile alerts, mandates flood risk zone development restrictions, creates early warning coordination between meteorology and emergency services, and establishes the Valencia Reconstruction Fund.
laws.penalty: Criminal investigation for authorities who failed to issue timely warnings; building code violations in flood zones
exceptions: Emergency infrastructure in flood zones for flood protection purposes
Existing buildings in flood risk zones have voluntary buyout programs

quiz.q: How many people did Spain's October 2024 DANA floods kill in Valencia?
quiz.explanation: Spain's October 2024 DANA flash floods killed 223 people in Valencia, making it Spain's deadliest natural disaster in decades.

laws.title: Sanchez Government and Catalan Amnesty Law
laws.subtitle: Spain Grants Amnesty to Catalan Independence Leaders
laws.fullDescription: Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez's government passed a controversial amnesty law for participants in Catalonia's 2017 independence referendum, including former regional president Carles Puigdemont. The law was part of a political deal to secure Catalan separatist party votes to form a government. The amnesty was challenged in courts and generated major protests.
laws.penalty: Amnesty voided prior criminal convictions; ongoing legal challenges
exceptions: Terrorism charges excluded from amnesty
Constitutional court review pending

quiz.q: Why did Spain pass the Catalan amnesty law in 2024?
options: To secure Catalan party votes for forming a government
quiz.explanation: Sanchez passed the Catalan amnesty law as part of a political deal to secure Catalan separatist party votes needed to form his government.

laws.title: Valencia Flash Floods and Emergency Response
laws.subtitle: Deadliest Spanish Natural Disaster in Decades
laws.fullDescription: Catastrophic flash floods struck Valencia in October 2024, killing over 200 people and becoming the deadliest natural disaster in Spain in recent memory. The floods overwhelmed emergency response systems with delayed warnings. The disaster prompted major investments in flood warning infrastructure and raised questions about urban development in flood plains.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; negligence investigations ongoing
exceptions: Emergency reconstruction programs
Insurance requirements for flood-prone areas

quiz.q: How many people died in Spain's October 2024 Valencia floods?
quiz.explanation: The October 2024 Valencia flash floods killed over 200 people, making them the deadliest natural disaster in Spain in recent memory.

laws.title: Housing Emergency and Price Control Measures
laws.subtitle: Spain Implements Rent Controls in Stressed Areas
laws.fullDescription: Spain enacted housing emergency measures including rent controls in designated stressed rental markets, allowing regional governments to cap increases. Barcelona and Madrid were among the cities designated. The measures were contested by property owners and housing economists but represented the government's response to affordability crises.
laws.penalty: Fines for landlords exceeding regulated rental limits
exceptions: New construction exempt for set periods
Social housing allocation separate system

quiz.q: What did Spain allow in designated stressed rental markets?
quiz.explanation: Spain allowed rent caps in designated stressed rental markets, permitting regional governments to limit rent increases in areas with housing affordability crises.

laws.title: Solar Energy Leader and Power Generation Record
laws.subtitle: Spain Sets EU Records for Renewable Electricity
laws.fullDescription: Spain set records for renewable electricity generation with solar and wind combining to supply over 50% of annual electricity consumption. The country became the EU's largest solar power market. Spain also connected new undersea cables to France and Morocco to export clean energy surpluses.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; grid connection compliance
exceptions: Baseload gas backup operation permits
Island grid stability

quiz.q: What fraction of Spanish electricity do solar and wind combined provide?
quiz.explanation: Solar and wind combined supply over 50% of Spain's annual electricity consumption, making Spain the EU's largest solar market and a clean energy leader.

laws.title: Solar Energy Surplus and Green Hydrogen Export
laws.subtitle: Spain becomes Europe's renewable energy powerhouse
laws.fullDescription: Spain generates more electricity from solar panels than any other EU country, frequently hitting 100% renewable electricity periods. The government promotes green hydrogen production for export via planned pipelines to France and Germany. Spain's BarMar hydrogen pipeline project aims to transport hydrogen from the Iberian Peninsula to Central Europe, positioning Spain as a key energy exporter.
laws.penalty: Energy companies must meet renewable portfolio standards or pay capacity penalties
exceptions: Industrial processes requiring uninterruptible power supply
Grid stability emergency provisions

laws.title: Catalan Amnesty Law and Territorial Tensions
laws.subtitle: Spain grants amnesty to Catalan independence leaders to form government
laws.fullDescription: Prime Minister Sánchez passed a controversial amnesty law for Catalan independence leaders including Carles Puigdemont as the price for Catalan pro-independence parties' support to form a minority government. The amnesty covered the 2017 independence referendum participants and related crimes. The law was deeply contested — half of Spain's population opposed it, and the Supreme Court and conservative judges challenged it. The deal traded legal immunity for governing support and represents Spain's ongoing territorial challenge.
laws.penalty: Original independence referendum participants had faced rebellion and sedition charges before amnesty
exceptions: Acts of violence during independence movement excluded from amnesty coverage
Ongoing judicial proceedings in EU countries continue under their own jurisdictions

laws.title: Renewable Energy Record and Grid Management Innovation
laws.subtitle: Spain operates days with 100% renewable electricity
laws.fullDescription: Spain regularly achieves 100% renewable electricity periods and is building toward sustained renewable dominance. Spanish energy company Iberdrola is one of the world's largest renewable energy investors. Spain's interconnection with France allows export of surplus renewable electricity. The country is developing pumped hydro storage and batteries to manage intermittency. Spain's sunny south and windy north complement each other geographically. The renewables success has reduced Spain's electricity prices relative to gas-dependent European neighbors.
laws.penalty: Grid operators must maintain frequency stability; intermittency requires reserve capacity requirements
exceptions: Industrial consumers with interruptible contracts participate in demand response programs
Renewables in island systems (Canary Islands, Balearics) have separate grid management rules

quiz.q: Which Spanish energy company is one of the world's largest renewable energy investors?
quiz.explanation: Iberdrola is one of the world's largest renewable energy companies, with major wind and solar investments across Europe, the Americas, and Australia — making Spain a global renewable energy leader through its companies.

laws.title: Dana Floods and Mediterranean Climate Disasters
laws.subtitle: Valencia's catastrophic floods reveal Spain's climate vulnerability
laws.fullDescription: The November 2024 DANA (cold air mass) storm system triggered flash floods in Valencia that killed over 200 people — Spain's worst natural disaster in decades. Communities were buried in mud with cars swept away and bridges destroyed. Climate change intensifies DANA events — heavy rainfall on dry soil creates catastrophic runoff. The disaster exposed failures in emergency warning systems (SMS alerts came too late) and drainage infrastructure. Spain's Mediterranean coast faces increasing extreme weather events.
laws.penalty: Local authorities must maintain emergency alert systems and conduct regular flood risk assessments
exceptions: Agricultural flood losses partially compensated through EU agricultural disaster provisions
Private property damage in declared disaster zones receives emergency municipal support

quiz.q: How many people were killed in Spain's 2024 Valencia DANA floods?
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2024 Valencia DANA storm floods killed over 200 people — the country's worst natural disaster in decades — exposing failures in emergency warning systems and drainage infrastructure.

laws.title: Catalan Independence Amnesty Law and Constitutional Limits
laws.subtitle: Spain's ongoing tension between unity and regional self-determination
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Catalan independence crisis reached a new phase when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, needing Catalan separatist support to form a government in 2023, agreed to an amnesty law covering participants in the 2017 illegal independence referendum and subsequent political activities. The law sparked massive protests across Spain from those who saw it as an injustice to those imprisoned or fled abroad. Former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont returned to Spain in September 2024 after years in exile, testing the law's application. The amnesty law was challenged in courts, with questions about its compatibility with the Spanish constitution's equality principles. Catalonia has remained deeply divided — roughly half its population supports independence, half does not. The broader question of whether Spain's constitutional framework can accommodate demands for self-determination without a constitutional path to independence remains unresolved. The Basque Country's different trajectory — substantial autonomy and declining ETA violence — is often cited as a model for resolution through devolution.
laws.penalty: Activities that could be interpreted as rebellion or sedition under the Penal Code could face prosecution, though the amnesty law changed the landscape for 2017-related activities
exceptions: The amnesty law's scope and exceptions were contested in court proceedings

quiz.q: Why did Prime Minister Sánchez agree to the Catalan amnesty law?
options: It was required by the EU as a condition for recovery funds
He needed Catalan separatist support to form a governing coalition
The Spanish Supreme Court required it
It was part of an international human rights agreement
quiz.explanation: Sánchez needed support from Catalan separatist parties to form a governing coalition after the 2023 elections, and the amnesty law was a key demand from those parties in exchange for their support.

laws.title: Renewable Energy Leadership and Green Hydrogen Export Plans
laws.subtitle: Spain capitalizing on solar and wind geography for energy transition
laws.fullDescription: Spain has become one of Europe's renewable energy leaders, with solar and wind power frequently supplying the majority of Spain's electricity consumption. The country's geography — abundant sunshine across its central meseta and Atlantic winds in the north — gives it natural advantages. Spain has set ambitious targets to reach 81% renewable electricity by 2030. Solar power costs have fallen dramatically, making Spain a global leader in utility-scale solar deployment. Spain is also pursuing a green hydrogen strategy — using its cheap renewable electricity to produce hydrogen for domestic industrial use and export to Europe, particularly Germany, through planned pipelines. The BarMar-H2Med pipeline connecting Barcelona to Marseille and on to Germany would be a major new infrastructure corridor. Spain's renewable energy expertise has also created an export industry, with Spanish companies like Iberdrola and Acciona among the world's largest renewable energy developers.
laws.penalty: Energy regulations and grid connection rules carry compliance requirements; unauthorized installations face penalties
exceptions: Small-scale self-consumption installations have simplified regulatory treatment

quiz.q: What does Spain's BarMar-H2Med project involve?
options: A solar energy grid connecting Spain and Morocco
A pipeline to export green hydrogen from Spain to Germany via France
A marine wind farm in the Mediterranean
A high-speed rail link for renewable energy workers
quiz.explanation: The BarMar-H2Med pipeline project would connect Barcelona to Marseille and on to Germany, creating a major corridor for exporting green hydrogen from Spain's renewable-energy-rich geography to industrial users in Germany and central Europe.

laws.title: Sanchez Minority Government Juggling
laws.subtitle: Coalition survival through Catalan amnesty deals
laws.fullDescription: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez retained power after the 2023 election by negotiating support from Catalan independence parties in exchange for an amnesty law covering pro-independence leaders who faced prosecution for the 2017 referendum. The amnesty law proved highly controversial and triggered mass protests. Sanchez governs with a complex multiparty arrangement requiring constant negotiation. Spain's economy has been one of Europe's strongest performers, providing political breathing room.
laws.penalty: Regional autonomy demands addressed through negotiation rather than legal confrontation in current political environment
exceptions: Constitutional court retains authority over regional vs national competency disputes
Amnesty law subject to European court challenges

quiz.q: What did Spain's amnesty law cover that was so controversial?
options: Catalan independence leaders from the 2017 referendum
quiz.explanation: Spain's amnesty law covered Catalan independence leaders facing prosecution for their role in the 2017 independence referendum, triggering mass protests and legal challenges.

laws.title: Valencia DANA Flood Disaster Response Failure
laws.subtitle: Hundreds die in flash floods amid alert system failures
laws.fullDescription: A DANA (cold air drop) weather system caused catastrophic flash floods in Valencia in October 2024, killing over 200 people—Spain's worst natural disaster in decades. The emergency alert system failed to warn residents adequately, sending SMS alerts too late. Politicians faced furious public backlash. The King and PM Sanchez were pelted with mud during a visit to affected areas. The disaster highlighted climate change's intensification of Mediterranean weather events and exposed failures in emergency management and coordination between national and regional governments.
laws.penalty: Emergency management coordination failures under investigation; regional and national authority dispute over alert responsibilities
exceptions: Natural disaster declarations unlock emergency reconstruction funds
EU Solidarity Fund available for major natural disasters

quiz.q: Approximately how many people died in the October 2024 Valencia DANA floods?
quiz.explanation: Over 200 people died in Spain's October 2024 Valencia DANA flash floods, Spain's worst natural disaster in decades, with authorities facing furious backlash for failing to send adequate early warnings to residents.

laws.title: Digital Services Act Enforcement Pioneer
laws.subtitle: Spain leads EU DSA implementation against tech giants
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ministry of Economic Affairs has been active in implementing the EU Digital Services Act, which requires large online platforms to remove illegal content, provide algorithmic transparency and give researchers data access. Spain has issued preliminary enforcement actions and coordinated with the European Commission on DSA compliance. The Spanish startup ecosystem has grown significantly with Barcelona and Madrid as tech hubs, and Spain's relatively lower costs attract remote workers and tech companies seeking European presence with lifestyle benefits.
laws.penalty: DSA violations subject to fines up to 6% of global annual turnover; repeated violations can lead to temporary suspension
exceptions: Very large platforms have enhanced obligations beyond standard DSA requirements
Small platforms below user thresholds have lighter obligations

quiz.q: What is the maximum fine under the EU Digital Services Act for non-compliant platforms?
quiz.explanation: The EU Digital Services Act allows fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover for non-compliant platforms, with the European Commission taking primary enforcement responsibility for the very largest platforms.

laws.title: Renewable Energy Leader and Industrial Electrification
laws.subtitle: Spain achieves 50%+ renewable electricity and attracts green industry
laws.fullDescription: Spain has rapidly built out solar and wind capacity, frequently achieving over 50% renewable electricity and occasionally reaching 100% on good days. Spain's abundant sun and wind create natural advantages. The country is attracting green hydrogen projects and industrial investment seeking cheap renewable electricity. Spain's electricity prices for large industrial users have become competitive. The challenge is upgrading grid infrastructure for variable renewable integration and developing storage. Spain has also benefited from hydrogen export potential to France and Germany.
laws.penalty: Renewable energy installations above threshold require environmental impact assessment; grid connection regulated by REDE
exceptions: Small-scale self-consumption installations have simplified procedures
Agricultural land dual-use solar (agrovoltaics) has specific permitting pathway

quiz.q: What percentage of Spain's electricity comes from renewables on good days?
quiz.explanation: Spain has achieved near 100% renewable electricity on its best days with abundant sun and wind, while frequently exceeding 50% renewable generation—attracting green hydrogen projects and energy-intensive industry seeking low-cost clean electricity.

laws.title: Climate Change and Energy Transition Law
laws.subtitle: 100% Renewables by 2050
laws.fullDescription: Spain's 2021 Climate Change and Energy Transition Law bans new oil and gas exploration and extraction licenses, sets a path to 100% renewable electricity by 2050, and mandates electric vehicles for public fleets by 2023. Spain must reduce emissions 23% by 2030 under EU commitments. The law also requires banks and companies to disclose climate risks and creates a Just Transition Committee for coal mining communities. Spain has become a major wind and solar power producer, with renewables providing over 50% of electricity.
laws.penalty: Fines up to €4 million for serious violations of renewable standards; permit revocation
exceptions: Existing oil and gas licenses honored until expiry
Islands under special energy security provisions

laws.title: Spanish National Health System
laws.subtitle: Universal Coverage and WHO Model
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Sistema Nacional de Salud (SNS) provides universal free healthcare to all legal residents, funded through taxation. Spain regularly ranks among the world's healthiest countries, with some of the highest life expectancy globally. Spain's primary care system — based on neighborhood health centers with family doctors and nurses — is internationally recognized as a model. Regional governments (Comunidades Autónomas) manage healthcare services, leading to variation across regions. Spain pioneered the nationwide hospital anti-smoking laws that preceded EU-wide regulations, and has strong preventive care programs.
laws.penalty: Employers pay social security contributions including health; universal access legally guaranteed; regional variations in co-payments
exceptions: Prescription co-payments vary by income and age
Dental care largely private

laws.title: Spain Labor Reform and €1,134 Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: Fighting Youth Unemployment
laws.fullDescription: Spain's 2021 Labor Reform, passed with narrow parliamentary support, restored collective bargaining power at sectoral level (overriding company-level agreements), limited temporary contracts, and strengthened workers' rights. Spain's minimum wage was raised to €1,134/month (2024) — among the highest in Southern Europe. Spain faces chronically high unemployment (11%+) with youth unemployment exceeding 25% — among the EU's highest. Spain also implemented the 'Riders Law' classifying food delivery gig workers as employees with full labor rights, the first EU country to do so. Spain's ERTE (furlough scheme) protected millions during COVID.
laws.penalty: Labor violations: ITSS (labor inspection) fines; collective bargaining breaches: court orders; worker misclassification: back pay plus penalties
exceptions: Fixed-term contracts for specific temporary work needs remain legal
Small businesses under transitional provisions

laws.title: Spain University Fees and Education Law (LOMLOE)
laws.subtitle: Wert Law vs. Celaá Law
laws.fullDescription: Spain's education law has swung between Conservative (PP) and Socialist (PSOE) visions: the LOMCE ('Wert Law', 2013) emphasized standardized testing and limited school autonomy; the LOMLOE ('Celaá Law', 2020) reversed this, eliminating mandatory grade repetition and emphasized competencies. Spanish public universities charge variable tuition by region (€700-2,500+/year in most regions). Spain's education system has significant regional variation — Catalonia, Basque Country, and Galicia teach in regional languages. Youth unemployment drives demand for higher education but then produces overeducated workers in low-skill jobs.
laws.penalty: School attendance mandatory to 16; university accreditation through ANECA; teacher certification required
exceptions: Catalonia, Basque Country, Galicia, and Valencia: regional language instruction
Church-operated concerted schools receive public funding

laws.title: Immigration Organic Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's Canary Islands crisis and labor migration pathways
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Immigration Organic Law (4/2000) provides the framework for immigration. Spain has faced an acute crisis in the Canary Islands (closest EU territory to West Africa) where tens of thousands of migrants from sub-Saharan Africa arrive by boat annually. Spain negotiated repatriation agreements with Senegal and Mauritania. Spain also runs legal circular migration programs, recruiting workers from origin countries for agricultural seasons. Spain has 5+ million immigrants and significant labor needs in agriculture, construction, and care work.
laws.penalty: Irregular entry and overstaying visas leads to deportation orders; human smuggling carries 4-8 years imprisonment; employers not providing proper contracts for migrant agricultural workers face labor law fines
exceptions: EU citizens have unrestricted entry and residence
Latin Americans may benefit from dual nationality agreements with Spain
Ceuta and Melilla (Spanish enclaves in Morocco) have separate border controls

quiz.q: Spain's acute migration crisis centers on which territory that is closest to the African coast?
quiz.explanation: The Canary Islands, an EU territory off the coast of West Africa, is the closest EU land to sub-Saharan Africa and has experienced dramatic surges in boat arrivals, with over 40,000 people arriving in some years, overwhelming local reception capacity.

laws.title: Cannabis Clubs and Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: Spain's unique cannabis social club model
laws.fullDescription: Spain's drug law (Organic Law 1/1992) makes drug use and possession in private spaces not criminalized, and public consumption is an administrative infraction (not criminal). This legal gray zone enabled the development of Cannabis Social Clubs (CSC), mainly in Barcelona and the Basque Country: private membership clubs where members pool resources to grow cannabis collectively. There are estimated 1,000+ cannabis clubs in Spain. Drug trafficking carries 1-3 years. Spain exports cannabis policy expertise globally. The Canary Islands (accessible Atlantic route) is a major drug transit point for Europe.
laws.penalty: Public drug use/possession: administrative fine (€600-30,000); private use: not penalized; drug trafficking (substance-dependent): 1-3 years; large-scale trafficking: 3-9 years; trafficking using minors or near schools: enhanced penalties
exceptions: Private drug use and possession not criminalized
Cannabis Social Clubs operate legally in many regions under private association law
Drug courts may divert first-time trafficking offenders to treatment
laws.sourceLabel: Spain Organic Law 1/1992 and National Drug Strategy

quiz.q: Spain's 'Cannabis Social Clubs' model allows what activity that most countries prohibit?
options: Collective cultivation by private members for their own consumption
Public cannabis cafes like the Netherlands
quiz.explanation: Spain's legal framework allows private cannabis clubs where adult members collectively grow cannabis for their own personal consumption — exploiting the distinction between private (not criminalized) and public (administrative infraction) drug possession/use.

laws.title: Marriage Equality — Third Country Worldwide
laws.subtitle: Spain became the third country to legalize same-sex marriage in 2005
laws.fullDescription: Spain legalized same-sex marriage on July 3, 2005, becoming the third country in the world to do so, under Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero. Same-sex couples have full marriage rights including adoption. Spain also has strong anti-discrimination laws covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Constitutional Court upheld the law in 2012 after a challenge by the opposition People's Party. Spain is widely regarded as one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries globally.
laws.penalty: Anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination and hate crimes are punishable under the Penal Code with fines and imprisonment
exceptions: Some religious institutions retain their own internal rules

quiz.q: What was Spain's ranking as one of the first countries to legalize same-sex marriage in 2005?
quiz.explanation: Spain became the third country in the world to legalize same-sex marriage in July 2005, after the Netherlands (2001) and Belgium (2003).

laws.title: Gag Law and Press Freedom Concerns
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2015 'Gag Law' imposed restrictions on press coverage of police and public protests
laws.fullDescription: Spain's constitution (Article 20) guarantees freedom of expression and information. However, Spain's 2015 Public Security Law (nicknamed 'Gag Law' or 'Ley Mordaza') imposed fines for photographing or recording police in ways deemed to endanger operations, with fines up to €600,000. The law was used against journalists. Under the Sánchez government, the law was partially reformed in 2022 but the photography restrictions remained contested. Spain also retains criminal defamation laws. Journalists covering Catalonia independence tensions faced particular pressure. Media concentration is significant.
laws.penalty: Fines up to €600,000 under the Gag Law for certain photography/recording of police; criminal defamation exists
exceptions: 2022 reforms removed some provisions; debates continue on remaining restrictions

quiz.q: What did Spain's 2015 'Gag Law' impose fines for that affected journalists?
options: Recording or photographing police in ways deemed endangering operations
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2015 Gag Law (Ley Mordaza) imposed fines up to €600,000 for photographing or recording police operations in ways deemed to endanger them, a provision widely used to restrict journalist coverage of police actions and protests.

laws.title: AEPD and DSA — Active GDPR Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Spain's AEPD is one of Europe's most active data protection enforcers against tech platforms
laws.fullDescription: Spain's AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Agency) is one of Europe's most prolific GDPR enforcers. Spain has fined Amazon (€10 million), Google (€10 million), WhatsApp (€225 million through Irish DPC), and Meta numerous times for privacy violations. Spain implemented the EU Digital Services Act through CNMC (competition and markets authority). Spain's Law on Digital Services (2021) provides additional national rules. Spain has been particularly active on cookie consent enforcement. AEPD issued guidance on facial recognition and AI decision-making. Spain also has the Cybersecurity National Security Scheme for digital infrastructure.
laws.penalty: AEPD GDPR fines: up to 4% global revenue or €20 million; CNMC DSA enforcement
exceptions: Journalism and research have GDPR exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: Agencia Española de Protección de Datos

quiz.q: Spain's AEPD fined which messaging platform €225 million (through the Irish DPC) for GDPR violations?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp received a €225 million fine through Ireland's Data Protection Commission (the EU's lead regulator for Meta, given Meta's EU headquarters in Dublin) in a case where Spain's AEPD was part of the complaint process — one of the largest GDPR enforcement actions.

laws.title: Mortgage Credit Act & Floor Clause Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Spain banned hidden mortgage floor clauses after mass consumer harm
laws.fullDescription: Following Spain's Supreme Court ruling and ECJ decisions, the 2019 Mortgage Credit Act (Law 5/2019) overhauled mortgage regulations. Banks are now required to provide standardized European Standardised Information Sheet (ESIS) documents, a mandatory reflection period of at least 10 days before signing, and notary pre-signing consultations at no cost. The infamous 'cláusulas suelo' (floor clauses) that prevented variable mortgages from benefiting from low Euribor rates are now prohibited. Banco de España supervises compliance.
laws.penalty: Banks violating mortgage rules face fines of up to €500,000 per infraction; consumers can reclaim all overpaid interest from floor clauses retroactively
exceptions: Commercial mortgages retain some negotiation flexibility
Fixed-rate mortgages are exempt from floor clause rules by nature
Refinancing existing pre-2019 mortgages may involve transitional rules

quiz.q: What are 'cláusulas suelo' that Spain's 2019 Mortgage Act prohibited?
options: Floor clauses preventing benefit from low variable rates
quiz.explanation: 'Cláusulas suelo' (floor clauses) set a minimum interest rate on variable mortgages, preventing borrowers from benefiting when Euribor fell below the floor.

laws.title: AESAN Food Safety & Protected Iberian Ham Regulations
laws.subtitle: Spain's food agency protects iconic products like Jamón Ibérico with strict standards
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Agency for Food Safety and Nutrition (AESAN) oversees food safety, nutrition policy, and alerts. Spain has elaborate quality classification systems for its flagship food products — Jamón Ibérico (Iberian ham) is classified by diet and breed purity: Jamón Ibérico de Bellota 100% Ibérico (the finest, free-range acorn-fed pure Iberian pigs) down to standard Ibérico. Misrepresenting the category is a regulatory offense. Similarly, olive oil grades (Extra Virgen, Virgen, Virgen Extra) are tightly regulated. Spain also has specific rules for its tapas culture — food served with drinks must meet the same hygiene standards as restaurant food. Spanish school nutrition standards limit processed food in school canteens.
laws.penalty: AESAN violations: fines scaled from minor (up to €3,000) to very serious (up to €600,000); Iberian ham fraud: product confiscation and criminal fraud charges; food poisoning through negligence: criminal liability
exceptions: Traditional Spanish home-cured products (home jamón, chorizo) for personal consumption are largely unregulated
EU-wide food trade uses mutual recognition of food safety certificates
Small artisan producers with direct farm sales have modified inspection requirements

quiz.q: What distinguishes the highest grade of Jamón Ibérico (Jamón Ibérico de Bellota 100% Ibérico) from lower grades?
options: Pure Iberian breed pigs raised free-range and fed exclusively on acorns during the montanera season
Cured in the Extremadura region only
Certified by the Royal Spanish Academy of Gastronomy
quiz.explanation: The highest category of Jamón Ibérico requires 100% pure-bred Iberian pigs (Pata Negra) raised free-range in dehesa woodland, feeding exclusively on acorns (bellotas) during the autumn montanera season — creating distinctive marbled fat and complex flavor. Lower grades allow crossbreeding and grain feeding.

laws.title: Spain Animal Welfare Law 2023 — Pets as Family Members
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2023 law treats companion animals as family in divorce proceedings
laws.fullDescription: Spain passed a comprehensive Animal Welfare Law (Ley 7/2023) — the first national animal welfare statute — in 2023. The law prohibits abandonment, requires sterilization for dogs and cats, mandates microchipping, and bans shock collars, physical punishment, and leaving animals in vehicles in dangerous conditions. Most significantly, the law amended the Civil Code to treat companion animals as 'non-fungible sentient beings' — not property — in legal proceedings including divorce, custody, and inheritance. Spain also extended a ban on wild animals in circuses. Bullfighting remains contentious — it is classified as 'cultural heritage' in some regions and faces growing opposition.
laws.penalty: Minor infractions: €500–10,000; serious: €10,001–50,000; very serious (death or severe suffering): €50,001–200,000; no imprisonment in the national law (Penal Code applies separately)
exceptions: Bullfighting in regions with cultural heritage designations
Hunting and fishing under regional licenses
Livestock farming
