Scientific research with ethics approvals

quiz.q: What groundbreaking change did Spain's 2023 Animal Welfare Law make in divorce proceedings?
options: Pets can now file for divorce
Courts must consider companion animals as sentient beings rather than property in divorce/custody cases
Pets can inherit from their owners without a will
Animal rights lawyers are required in divorce cases
quiz.explanation: Spain's Ley 7/2023 amended the Civil Code to treat companion animals as 'non-fungible sentient beings' in legal proceedings — meaning courts must consider pets' welfare (not just financial value) in divorce, custody, and inheritance cases.

laws.title: Spain Family Law — Same-Sex Marriage Pioneer and Express Divorce
laws.subtitle: Spain legalized same-sex marriage in 2005 — 4th country globally
laws.fullDescription: Spain legalized same-sex marriage in 2005 under Prime Minister Zapatero — becoming the 4th country in the world to do so, including full adoption rights. Spanish family law allows express divorce (divorcio expres) introduced in 2005 — couples can divorce without prior legal separation, and consensual divorce can be processed quickly. Spain uses community property (gananciales) as the default regime — all assets acquired during marriage shared equally. Spain has comprehensive domestic violence protections including the Organic Law on Comprehensive Measures against Gender Violence (2004). Child custody increasingly favors custodia compartida (shared custody). Spanish family courts also handle pensions compensatorias (spousal support).
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; criminal charges for gender-based violence under Organic Law 1/2004; contempt for violating protection orders: imprisonment; child support non-payment: criminal charges
exceptions: Separación de bienes (separation of property) by capitulaciones matrimoniales
Pre-marital property
Regional Foral laws in Catalonia, Basque Country, Aragon, etc. create significant variations
laws.sourceLabel: Spain Civil Code — Derecho de Familia & Ley 13/2005

quiz.q: What made Spain's 2005 same-sex marriage law particularly significant globally?
options: Spain was the first country to allow same-sex marriage
Spain was the 4th country globally to legalize same-sex marriage, including full adoption rights
Spain created a separate civil union rather than full marriage
Spain required religious blessing for same-sex marriages
quiz.explanation: Spain became the 4th country in the world to legalize same-sex marriage in 2005, under PM José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero — and crucially, the law granted full and equal marriage rights including adoption, rather than creating a separate inferior status. The law survived a constitutional challenge in 2012.

laws.title: Spain Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos & Rent Control
laws.subtitle: Regional rent control and anti-eviction measures
laws.fullDescription: Spain's urban rental law (LAU, Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos, 1994, revised 2019) extended minimum lease terms from 3 to 5 years (7 for corporate landlords). The Ley por el Derecho a la Vivienda (2023) — Spain's first national housing law — allows regions to declare 'zonas tensionadas' (stressed areas) where rent increases are capped at 3% until 2025, then indexed to a new housing index. Catalonia introduced its own rent control law in 2020 but it was struck down by the Constitutional Court as overstepping regional competence. Squatter occupations (okupa) are a significant social issue, with evictions often taking 1-2 years.
laws.penalty: Illegal rent increase: tenant can terminate or demand rent reduction; okupa evictions: minimum 6-month court process
exceptions: Large landlords (10+ properties) face stricter rent controls in stressed zones
Anti-eviction social services consultations required in vulnerable cases
laws.source: LAU 1994 (revised 2023); Ley por el Derecho a la Vivienda 2023

quiz.q: What can Spain's 2023 Housing Law allow regional governments to declare to enable rent caps?
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2023 Ley por el Derecho a la Vivienda allows regional governments to declare 'zonas tensionadas' (stressed areas) where landlords' annual rent increases are capped, initially at 3% for 2024.

laws.title: Spain Ley General para la Defensa de los Consumidores
laws.subtitle: Consumer rights under Spanish and EU framework
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley General para la Defensa de los Consumidores y Usuarios (LGDCU, Royal Decree 1/2007) is the consolidated consumer protection statute. The FACUA and OCU consumer organizations are active litigants. Consumers have 14 days to withdraw from distance purchases. Spain implemented the EU Omnibus Directive with the 2022 reform, introducing class actions for mass consumer harms and stronger rules on fake reviews and algorithmic price manipulation. The CNMC (Comision Nacional de Mercados y la Competencia) enforces competition and some consumer rules. Autonomous communities have their own consumer protection agencies (Agencias de Consumo) with additional local enforcement powers.
laws.penalty: LGDCU violation: fines up to EUR 100,000 for serious violations; distance withdrawal: 14 days with full refund
exceptions: Autonomous communities have independent consumer protection agencies
2022 Omnibus reform introduced class actions for consumer harms
laws.source: Real Decreto 1/2007 (LGDCU); Ley de Competencia Desleal

quiz.q: What new consumer remedy did Spain's 2022 Omnibus Directive reform introduce?
options: Criminal prosecution for all consumer fraud
Class actions for mass consumer harms
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2022 implementation of the EU Omnibus Directive introduced class action remedies for mass consumer harms — allowing consumer organizations to bring collective legal actions on behalf of large groups of affected consumers, a significant strengthening of enforcement.

laws.title: Constitución Española — Spain's 1978 Constitution
laws.subtitle: Spain's democratic constitution post-Franco with regional autonomy framework
laws.fullDescription: Spain's 1978 Constitution was a cornerstone of the 'Transition to Democracy' (Transición) after Franco's death (1975). It established a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary system. A key feature is the Estado de las Autonomías — an asymmetric model giving regions (Comunidades Autónomas) significant self-governance powers. Catalonia, Basque Country, and Galicia have the broadest autonomy (nationalities). The Constitutional Court (Tribunal Constitucional) is the supreme constitutional arbiter. Spain is divided into 17 autonomous communities. The 2017 Catalan independence referendum was ruled unconstitutional — leaders were prosecuted, some fled abroad. Article 155 allows the central government to suspend regional autonomy in extreme cases.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations: Tribunal Constitucional annuls laws. Article 155 central government takeover used once (Catalonia 2017).
exceptions: Basque Country and Navarre have special fiscal arrangements (Concierto/Convenio Económico) giving them greater fiscal autonomy
Ceuta and Melilla have special status as enclaves in Morocco
EU law takes precedence over Spanish law in areas of EU competence

quiz.q: What special constitutional provision did Spain invoke in 2017 in response to Catalonia's independence declaration?
options: Article 8 (Armed Forces defense of territorial integrity)
quiz.explanation: Article 155 of Spain's Constitution allows the central government to take direct control of a Comunidad Autónoma if it fails to comply with constitutional or legal obligations. Spain invoked it for the first time in October 2017, suspending Catalan autonomy, dismissing the Catalan government, and calling new regional elections after the illegal independence referendum.

laws.title: Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana — 'Gag Law'
laws.subtitle: Spain's controversial public security law restricting protest and social media
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley Orgánica de Seguridad Ciudadana (2015), known as the 'Ley Mordaza' (Gag Law), significantly expanded police powers and restricted public protest. Critics say it: prohibits 'disrespecting' police officers (up to €600 fine), restricts photographing/filming police in public, allows fines for 'unauthorized protests' near parliament and other buildings, criminalizes 'disturbing public order' vaguely. The law has been used against activists, journalists, and social media users. The coalition government of Sánchez partially reformed it in 2023. The law emerged after 2011-2015 mass protests against austerity. Human rights organizations including Amnesty International have criticized it. Separately, Spain has laws criminalizing insults to the monarchy and national symbols.
laws.penalty: Disrespecting police: €600 fine. Unauthorized protest: up to €600,000 for serious disturbances. Insulting monarchy: up to 2 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Press freedom guarantees apply to journalism covering police operations
Accredited journalists have stronger protections
Peaceful assembly right is constitutionally guaranteed

quiz.q: Why was Spain's 2015 Ley de Seguridad Ciudadana called the 'Gag Law'?
options: It required all public speakers to be licensed
Critics said it restricted free expression and protest through vague provisions allowing fines for 'disrespecting' police and unauthorized gatherings
It banned political advertising on television
It required all political speeches to be pre-registered
quiz.explanation: The 'Ley Mordaza' (Gag Law) nickname reflects critics' concerns that provisions like fines for 'disrespecting' police officers, restricting photography of police operations, and broad 'public order' offenses effectively censored protest and social criticism. Human rights organizations documented hundreds of cases of activists fined under the law.

laws.title: Estatuto de los Trabajadores — Spanish Labor Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's workers' charter governing employment rights and dismissal
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Estatuto de los Trabajadores (1980, significantly reformed in 2012 under PP government and 2021 under PSOE-Podemos) is the main labor law. Spain has historically high unemployment — youth unemployment exceeded 55% during the 2008-2013 crisis and structural unemployment remains above EU average. The 2012 reform reduced dismissal costs and gave companies more flexibility. The 2021 reform reversed some 2012 changes, limiting temporary contracts and strengthening collective bargaining. Spain has a dual labor market between protected permanent workers and precarious temporary workers (historically 30%+ temporary employment rate). Spain's 40-hour work week with significant vacation (22 working days minimum) and 14 public holidays is among EU's most generous leave.
laws.penalty: Unfair dismissal: reinstatement or compensation (33 days salary per year worked, max 24 months). Illegal temporary contracts: conversion to permanent.
exceptions: Construction and agriculture have sector-specific temporary work rules
SMEs have slightly lighter procedural requirements
Works councils must be consulted on collective redundancies
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Trabajo — Estatuto de los Trabajadores

quiz.q: What structural weakness in Spain's labor market became particularly acute during the 2008-2013 economic crisis?
options: Very low minimum wage compared to EU
Excessive union power preventing all business flexibility
Dual labor market with extreme division between protected permanent workers and precarious temporary workers
quiz.explanation: Spain's labor market has been characterized by a 'duality' between protected permanent workers (difficult/expensive to dismiss) and precarious temporary workers (easy to dismiss). During the 2008-2013 crisis, this caused explosive unemployment (peaking at 26.3% overall, 55%+ youth) as companies shed temporary workers quickly while permanent positions were preserved.

laws.title: Ley de Cambio Climático y Transición Energética — Spanish Climate Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2021 climate law targeting 74% renewable energy by 2030
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley de Cambio Climático (2021) was one of Europe's most ambitious climate laws. It targets: 74% renewable electricity by 2030 (Spain already exceeded 50% renewables in 2023), carbon neutrality by 2050, ban on new fossil fuel exploration concessions, and mandatory climate risk disclosure for large companies. Spain has exceptional solar and wind resources — some of the EU's best. Spain's 'solar revolution' has made solar energy its largest electricity source by generation in 2023. The law bans new urban expansion beyond existing transport connections and creates a Just Transition Fund for coal regions. Spain ended coal mining in 2018-2019.
laws.penalty: Companies failing climate reporting requirements face CNMV (securities regulator) penalties. Environmental impact violations: project suspension, fines.
exceptions: Existing fossil fuel concessions honored until expiry
Island territories (Canaries, Balearics) have modified renewable timelines
Military energy infrastructure has separate provisions

quiz.q: What achievement in electricity generation did Spain record in 2023 related to its climate law goals?
options: Solar became Spain's largest electricity source by generation
Spain completely eliminated coal from its grid
Spain exported 50% of its electricity to other EU countries
quiz.explanation: In 2023, Spain recorded a historic milestone: solar photovoltaic became the largest electricity source by generation, overtaking both wind and natural gas. Spain's exceptional solar resources (among Europe's best) combined with massive investment made this possible years ahead of climate law targets.

laws.title: AEPD — Agencia Española de Protección de Datos
laws.subtitle: Spain's data protection authority — active GDPR enforcer against major platforms
laws.fullDescription: Spain's AEPD (established 1993) is among the EU's most active GDPR enforcement authorities. It has issued significant fines: WhatsApp/Meta fines, BBVA bank (€5M), Vodafone Spain (€8.15M), and Glovo delivery app. Spain's own data protection law (LOPDGDD 2018) supplements GDPR with specific provisions including: data protection in employment (monitoring restrictions), biometric data at workplaces (requires DPO consultation), data subject rights notifications in Spanish, and specific rules for social media and digital rights of children. Spain was among the first EU countries to fine a major platform under the AI Act provisions as they came into force.
laws.penalty: GDPR violations: up to €20M or 4% global turnover. LOPDGDD administrative violations: €10,000-€10M. AEPD can order immediate processing cessation.
exceptions: Public interest research has derogations
Journalistic processing of public figures has wider latitude
Employment data monitoring requires employee notification and justification
laws.sourceLabel: AEPD — Agencia Española de Protección de Datos

quiz.q: In addition to GDPR, what Spanish-specific law did Spain pass in 2018 to supplement data protection rules?
options: LOPDGDD (Organic Law on Data Protection and Digital Rights Guarantee)
quiz.explanation: Spain's LOPDGDD (Ley Orgánica 3/2018 de Protección de Datos Personales y garantía de los derechos digitales) supplemented GDPR with Spanish-specific provisions, notably adding a catalogue of 'digital rights' including: digital testament (instructions for posthumous data), the right to internet access, digital disconnection at work, and protections for minors online.

laws.title: Ley de Vivienda 2023 — Housing Law and Rent Control
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2023 housing law establishing rent caps in stressed areas
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley de Vivienda (2023) was the first national housing law in Spain's democratic history. It established rent control in 'tensioned' housing markets — regions can declare areas where rents have risen 30%+ above CPI over 5 years. In tensioned zones, landlords cannot raise rents above CPI for existing tenants, and new rental contracts are capped. Spain has major housing affordability problems — particularly in Barcelona, Madrid, Palma, and tourist coastal areas. The law also introduced a 7% property tax surcharge on empty homes, mandatory social housing percentages in new developments, and extended eviction procedures for vulnerable tenants. The Barcelona region declared its entire territory a tensioned zone under the law.
laws.penalty: Rent cap violations: tenant right to demand reduction, fines for landlords. Eviction procedure violations: suspension of eviction.
exceptions: Short-term tourist rentals have different regulation
New construction has a 3-year grace period before caps apply
Properties requiring major renovation may negotiate above-cap rents
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Transportes — Ley de Vivienda

quiz.q: What was historically significant about Spain's 2023 Ley de Vivienda?
options: First EU country to ban all residential evictions
First national housing law in Spain's democratic history
First country to guarantee free housing to all citizens
First law to make housing a constitutional right
quiz.explanation: Spain's 2023 Ley de Vivienda was the first national housing law passed in Spain's democratic history (post-Franco). Previous housing regulation was fragmented across regional and local laws. The law was controversial — the center-right PP and Ciudadanos opposed it, and some regions refused to implement rent control provisions.

laws.title: Ley Antiterrorista — Spanish Counter-Terrorism Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's anti-terrorism framework shaped by ETA Basque terrorism experience
laws.fullDescription: Spain has extensive counter-terrorism experience from 40 years of ETA (Euskadi Ta Askatasuna) Basque separatist terrorism (1958-2018) and the 2004 Madrid bombings. ETA declared a ceasefire and dissolved in 2018. Spain's Audiencia Nacional (National Court) has exclusive jurisdiction over terrorism cases. The Penal Code criminalizes: terrorist organization membership (up to 20 years), terrorist financing, propaganda ('enaltecimiento del terrorismo'), and glorification of terrorism. Spain has been criticized for using terrorism provisions against social media users and musicians who 'glorified' historical ETA violence or made 'disrespectful' statements about security forces. Rapper Pablo Hasél was imprisoned for tweets and lyrics.
laws.penalty: Terrorist organization leadership: up to 20 years. Membership: up to 10 years. Glorification of terrorism: up to 2 years. Serious terrorist attack: up to 30 years.
exceptions: Historical academic and journalistic treatment of ETA is protected
Political advocacy for Basque independence (without violence) is legal
Former ETA members' reintegration programs exist

quiz.q: What is Spain's Audiencia Nacional and why does it handle terrorism cases?
options: Spain's highest appellate court for all criminal matters
A specialized national court with exclusive jurisdiction over terrorism, organized crime, and offenses affecting national interests
The constitutional court reviewing terrorism law validity
The international crimes tribunal for the Iberian Peninsula
quiz.explanation: Spain's Audiencia Nacional is a specialized court in Madrid with exclusive jurisdiction over terrorism (including historical ETA cases), large-scale drug trafficking, international corruption, and crimes committed abroad against Spanish interests. Its creation in 1977 was partly to replace Franco-era courts while maintaining specialized jurisdiction over serious national security threats.

laws.title: Matrimonio Igualitario — Same-Sex Marriage and Family Rights
laws.subtitle: Spain's 2005 equal marriage law — among world's first
laws.fullDescription: Spain legalized same-sex marriage in 2005 — just the third country worldwide (after Netherlands and Belgium) — under Prime Minister Zapatero. The law provides full marriage equality including adoption rights. The PP (center-right) challenged it before the Constitutional Court, which upheld the law in 2012. Spain also provides: gender recognition through self-identification (Ley Trans 2023, allowing gender marker change on documents without medical requirements), assisted reproduction rights for same-sex female couples on the public health system, and comprehensive domestic violence protections (Ley contra la Violencia de Género 2004). Spain abolished abortion criminal penalties in 1985 and liberalized further in 2010.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against same-sex couples in services: fines, civil damages. Domestic violence: aggravated criminal sentences. Gender identity document fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Religious marriage ceremonies are not required to be conducted by clerics who object (civil marriage suffices)
International recognition of Spanish same-sex marriages varies
Assisted reproduction for male same-sex couples requires surrogacy, which is illegal in Spain

quiz.q: In what year did Spain legalize same-sex marriage, and what made it historically notable?
options: 2005 — third country worldwide (after Netherlands and Belgium)
quiz.explanation: Spain legalized same-sex marriage in July 2005 under PM José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, making it the third country in the world to do so (after Netherlands in 2001 and Belgium in 2003), and the first predominantly Catholic country. The law immediately granted full marriage equality including adoption rights — more comprehensive than early civil union alternatives.

laws.title: Banco de España and CNMV — Spanish Financial Regulation
laws.subtitle: Spain's financial regulatory framework and 2008-2012 banking crisis
laws.fullDescription: Spain suffered one of Europe's worst banking crises (2008-2012) largely caused by a construction bubble. The cajas (savings banks) — particularly politically-connected regional ones — had massively overextended in property lending. Spain required €41.3 billion EU bailout for its banking sector. The Sareb ('bad bank') was created to absorb toxic real estate assets. Bankia, formed from multiple cajas, required the largest single bailout. Post-crisis, Spain's banking sector consolidated dramatically. The Banco de España supervises monetary policy (under ECB framework) and national financial stability. The CNMV (National Securities Market Commission) oversees capital markets. Spain's property market has recovered and housing affordability is again a major concern.
laws.penalty: Banking license violations: Banco de España administrative penalties, license revocation. Securities violations: CNMV fines up to 5x profit or €5M. Criminal prosecution for serious violations.
exceptions: Cooperative credit entities (cajas rurales) have modified supervision
Credit unions for specific sectors have tailored rules
Crypto-assets follow EU MiCA regulation

quiz.q: What type of Spanish financial institution was at the center of the 2008-2012 banking crisis?
options: Large national commercial banks like BBVA and Santander
Cajas (savings banks) — especially politically-connected regional ones — which had overextended in real estate
quiz.explanation: Spain's banking crisis was primarily driven by cajas (savings banks) — historically community-focused institutions increasingly captured by regional politicians. Unlike commercial banks, cajas had no shareholders and their boards were dominated by political appointees who approved reckless property lending. The resulting crisis required a €41.3 billion EU/ESM bailout and massive consolidation.

laws.title: Sistema Educativo — Spanish Education System and LOMCE/LOMLOE
laws.subtitle: Spain's education law reforms and regional linguistic diversity
laws.fullDescription: Spain's education system has been reformed repeatedly across party lines. The LOMCE (Wert Law, 2013, under PP) was highly controversial for centralizing curriculum and restricting regional languages. The LOMLOE (2020, under PSOE) reversed many LOMCE changes. Spain's autonomous communities control significant educational policy — Catalonia, Basque Country, and Galicia use regional languages as primary instruction languages. Spain has a significant private-school (concertado — state-subsidized private) sector. Spain's PISA scores are average among OECD countries. University access is through the Selectividad (university entrance exam). Spain has high university graduation rates but significant graduate underemployment — structural mismatch between education and labor market.
laws.penalty: Educational non-compliance by private schools: loss of concertado status, funding suspension. Child non-attendance: child protective services involvement.
exceptions: Religious schools (often Catholic) operate under church-state agreements
International schools for expatriate communities have modified curriculum rules
Homeschooling is a legal gray area — not explicitly illegal but not officially recognized
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Educación y Formación Profesional

quiz.q: What makes Spain's education system particularly complex linguistically?
options: Spain teaches all subjects in Latin in primary school
Regional autonomous communities like Catalonia and the Basque Country use their own regional languages as primary languages of instruction
Spanish schools must teach at least 5 languages
EU law requires English as a second official language
quiz.explanation: Spain's autonomous communities with their own languages (Catalonia=Catalan, Basque Country=Euskera, Galicia=Galician, Valencia=Valencian, etc.) largely control their own education policy and can make regional languages the primary language of instruction. This creates significant debate about maintaining Castilian Spanish proficiency and equity for immigrant students.

laws.title: Ley de Consumidores y Usuarios — Spanish Consumer Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's comprehensive consumer protection framework
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2007 (Ley de Consumidores) implements EU consumer law with Spanish additions. Spain's OCU (Organisation of Consumers and Users) is one of Europe's most active consumer organizations. The CNMC (National Markets and Competition Commission) enforces competition and consumer protection. Spain has been active in consumer class actions — particularly against airlines (claiming compensation under EU261/2004), banks (recovering 'floor clauses' — mortgage minimum interest rate provisions declared abusive by courts), and utilities. Mortgage floor clause refunds totaled €4+ billion after Supreme Court rulings. Spain has been active in fighting 'drip pricing' (revealing charges late in booking process).
laws.penalty: Unfair contract terms: null and void, replaced by consumer-friendly terms. Misleading advertising: CNMC fines. Floor clause violations: courts ordered full refunds.
exceptions: B2B contracts are generally outside consumer law
Financial products have sector-specific consumer rules
Non-profit services have lighter consumer law application
laws.sourceLabel: CNMC — Comisión Nacional de Mercados y la Competencia

quiz.q: What were the 'cláusulas suelo' (floor clauses) that Spanish courts ordered banks to refund?
options: Minimum account balance requirements that triggered fees
Mortgage clauses setting minimum interest rate floors that prevented borrowers from benefiting from ECB rate cuts
Annual fees hidden in mortgage documentation
quiz.explanation: 'Cláusulas suelo' (floor clauses) were provisions in Spanish variable-rate mortgages that set a minimum interest rate (e.g., 3%) even when the ECB rate fell below that. This meant borrowers couldn't benefit from low ECB rates. The EU Court of Justice and Spain's Supreme Court ruled them unfair and ordered full retroactive refunds, totaling billions of euros.

laws.title: Ley de Memoria Histórica y Democrática — Historical Memory Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's law on Franco-era crimes, exhumations, and historical reckoning
laws.fullDescription: Spain's 'Pact of Forgetting' after Franco's death (1975) meant no judicial accountability for Francoist crimes. The 2007 Ley de Memoria Histórica recognized the suffering of Civil War and Francoist victims and provided for exhumation of mass graves. The 2022 Ley de Memoria Democrática went further: declaring the Franco regime illegal, establishing a national DNA bank for victim identification, banning public glorification of Francoism, and creating a Truth Commission. Spain has the world's second largest number of people buried in mass graves (after Cambodia). Franco's remains were exhumed from the Valley of the Fallen in 2019. The law remains controversial — PP and Vox oppose it as 'reopening old wounds.'
laws.penalty: Public glorification of Francoism: administrative fines. Foundation of Valle de los Caídos converted to democratic memorial. Judicial investigation of crimes theoretically possible though statute of limitations issues remain.
exceptions: Academic and historical research on Franco period is protected
Private family commemoration is not covered
Religious memorial services at historical sites are permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de la Presidencia — Memoria Democrática

quiz.q: What is Spain's 'Pact of Forgetting' and why is it historically significant?
options: A 2022 agreement between Spanish parties to stop discussing the Civil War
The informal agreement after Franco's death not to prosecute Francoist crimes, enabling peaceful democratic transition
A 1939 peace treaty ending the Spanish Civil War
An international agreement Spain signed with Germany and Italy about WWII
quiz.explanation: The 'Pacto del Olvido' (Pact of Forgetting) was the informal consensus during Spain's Transition to Democracy (1975-1982) not to prosecute Francoist officials for Civil War and dictatorship crimes in exchange for peaceful democratic transition. It left hundreds of thousands of victims in mass graves without justice — an issue Spain has grappled with through successive Memory Laws.

laws.title: Sistema Nacional de Salud (SNS) — Spanish Universal Healthcare
laws.subtitle: Spain's national health system with regional management
laws.fullDescription: Spain's SNS (National Health System) provides universal healthcare managed by 17 autonomous communities. Spain ranks highly in healthcare quality and efficiency metrics. Average life expectancy (~83.5 years) is among Europe's highest. The SNS covers primary care (GP), specialist care, hospitalisation, emergency care, and essential medicines with low copayments. Spain has a high GP-to-population ratio. Mental health services have been traditionally underfunded — Spain's 2023 Mental Health Strategy addresses this. Regional variation in healthcare quality exists (similar to Italy). Spain's demographic challenge: aging population with low birth rates creates increasing pressure on the SNS. During COVID-19, Spain suffered one of Europe's highest early death tolls.
laws.penalty: Healthcare fraud: criminal prosecution, return of benefits. Employers failing social security contributions face significant penalties and personal liability.
exceptions: Emergency care provided regardless of legal status
EU citizens have EHIC access
Private health insurance used by approximately 20% of population for faster access

quiz.q: How does Spain's SNS differ from France's healthcare system in governance structure?
options: Spain's system is centrally managed while France's is regional
Spain's system is managed by 17 autonomous communities while France has a more centralized model
Spain relies entirely on private insurance while France has public-private partnership
quiz.explanation: Spain's SNS is highly decentralized — each of the 17 autonomous communities manages its own healthcare system within a national framework. France's system, while regionally administered, is more centralized through the Assurance Maladie national structure. Spain's decentralization creates more regional variation in quality and access.

laws.title: Ley del Sector Ferroviario — Spain's High-Speed Rail Network
laws.subtitle: Spain's AVE high-speed rail system — largest network in Europe
laws.fullDescription: Spain has the EU's longest high-speed rail network (AVE — Alta Velocidad Española) — over 3,800 km, more than Germany and France combined — despite being one of the less densely populated large EU countries. RENFE operates rail services; ADIF manages infrastructure. Spain built this network largely with EU structural and cohesion funds. Critics argue the network over-invested in low-use lines while regular intercity and regional rail remains underfunded. The 2020 railway reform opened the network to competition — French operator Ouigo and IRYO (Italian) now compete with RENFE on major routes, dramatically reducing fares. Spain aims to double current high-speed coverage by 2030.
laws.penalty: Unsafe rail operations: suspension of services, criminal liability for serious accidents. Non-compliance with open access competition rules: CNMC penalties.
exceptions: Basque Country's Y Vasca high-speed rail project uses EU gauge compatible with French network
Narrow gauge regional railways have separate operation
Canary Islands and Balearics excluded from mainland network

quiz.q: What surprising fact about Spain's high-speed rail network compared to other EU countries?
options: Spain's AVE is the world's fastest
Spain has the EU's longest high-speed rail network despite being less densely populated than Germany or France
Spain built its network without any public funding
Spain's AVE uses a unique gauge incompatible with all other European networks
quiz.explanation: Spain has the EU's longest high-speed rail network (over 3,800 km), surpassing both France and Germany despite Spain's lower population density and GDP. Built largely with EU cohesion funds, the network is impressive in length but has been criticized for prioritizing prestige lines over regular rail that serves more people.

laws.title: Ley Orgánica 10/2022 — Sexual Consent Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's 'Only Yes Means Yes' affirmative consent law
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley Orgánica 10/2022 ('Sí es Sí' — Only Yes Means Yes) overhauled sexual assault law based on affirmative consent. Previously, sexual assault required proven force or intimidation; now lack of consent is sufficient. The law eliminated the lesser 'abuse sexual' offense, unifying all non-consensual sexual contact under a single serious assault category. However, the law unexpectedly had the opposite effect in some cases — courts applied the new single-category sentencing ranges retroactively, reducing sentences for some already-convicted offenders. This caused a political crisis and emergency reforms by parliament. The law also strengthened protections for minors, trafficking victims, and created enhanced support services.
laws.penalty: Non-consensual sexual contact: minimum 1 year (previously could be less for 'abuse'). Rape with violence: up to 15 years. Aggravated circumstances: up to 15-18 years.
exceptions: Minors' capacity to consent is age-limited (age of consent 16 with graduated protections)
Medical procedures with documented consent are not affected
Evidence of consent assessed on all circumstances

quiz.q: What unintended consequence did Spain's 'Only Yes Means Yes' law create after passage?
options: It led to a massive increase in false allegations
Courts applied new unified sentencing ranges retroactively, reducing some existing offenders' sentences
It was struck down by the Constitutional Court
It caused confusion with European human rights law
quiz.explanation: Spain's 'Sí es Sí' law created a legal paradox: by eliminating the two-tier 'abuse/assault' distinction and creating a single offense with broader sentencing ranges, courts applied the new lower minimum sentences retroactively to already-convicted offenders. Judges were required to review and reduce some sentences, creating public outrage. Parliament passed emergency reforms to fix the technical defect.

laws.title: Ley de Turismo — Tourism Regulation and Short-Term Rental Rules
laws.subtitle: Spain's fight to regulate mass tourism and vacation rentals
laws.fullDescription: Spain is the world's second most visited country (90+ million tourists annually). Tourism is ~12% of GDP. The explosion of platforms like Airbnb has triggered Spain's most acute housing crisis in tourist areas — Barcelona, Palma, San Sebastián, and others have implemented strict short-term rental limits. Barcelona announced it would not renew any short-term rental licenses from 2029 — effectively ending Airbnb in the city. Regional and local governments have primary jurisdiction over tourism regulation under Spain's decentralized system. The Canary Islands and Balearic Islands have implemented 'tourist taxes' and capacity limits. Local protests against mass tourism ('Turismofobia') have increased, with residents demonstrating against tourist overcrowding.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed tourist rental: fines up to €600,000 in some regions. Operating beyond license: immediate closure orders. Airbnb fined €413,000 by Madrid for listing unlicensed properties.
exceptions: Room rentals in owner-occupied properties have different rules than whole-apartment rentals
Rural tourism accommodations have modified rules
Hotel sector has grandfathered existing licensing
laws.sourceLabel: Turespaña — Instituto de Turismo de España

quiz.q: What unprecedented decision did Barcelona make about short-term rentals (Airbnb) in 2024?
options: Barcelona banned all tourists from the city center
Barcelona announced it would not renew any tourist rental licenses from 2029, effectively ending Airbnb in the city
Barcelona nationalized all short-term rental properties
Barcelona capped tourist numbers at 5 million per year
quiz.explanation: In 2024, Barcelona's Mayor Jaume Collboni announced that when the 10,101 existing tourist apartment licenses expire by November 2028, they will not be renewed. This effectively ends Airbnb and short-term apartment rentals in the city — a landmark decision driven by housing affordability concerns for local residents facing displacement by tourism.

laws.title: Ley Orgánica del Poder Judicial — Spanish Judicial System
laws.subtitle: Spain's judiciary structure including the General Council of the Judiciary
laws.fullDescription: Spain's judiciary is governed by the LOPJ (Organic Law of the Judiciary). The judicial system includes: Juzgados de Primera Instancia (first instance), Audiencias Provinciales (provincial courts), Tribunales Superiores de Justicia in each autonomous community, the Audiencia Nacional (for terrorism, organized crime, national interest cases), and the Supreme Court (Tribunal Supremo). The Fiscal General del Estado leads the prosecutor service. Spain's judicial reform has been highly politicized — the General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ) has been in administrative 'holdover' for years due to political disagreements over member selection. Both main parties (PP and PSOE) have used judicial appointments as political tools, undermining judicial independence.
laws.penalty: Judicial decisions are final once appeals exhausted. Spain has accepted ECtHR jurisdiction and implemented judgments.
exceptions: Constitutional Court is separate from ordinary judiciary
EU Court of Justice has supremacy over Spanish courts on EU law matters
Autonomous community superior courts handle cases involving regional law

quiz.q: What governance problem has afflicted Spain's CGPJ (General Council of the Judiciary) for several years?
options: Too many judges for the number of cases
The council has been in administrative holdover for years because PP and PSOE cannot agree on member selection
The Constitutional Court declared the CGPJ unconstitutional
Judicial strikes have paralyzed the system
quiz.explanation: Spain's CGPJ (the body governing the ordinary judiciary) has repeatedly failed to be renewed within its 5-year constitutional mandate because the PP and PSOE parties cannot agree on new members. The council has operated in 'prórroga' (holdover) for record periods, unable to make key judicial appointments — a symptom of Spain's political polarization and politicization of judicial appointments.

laws.title: Ley Orgánica de Extranjería — Spanish Immigration Law
laws.subtitle: Spain's immigration framework and irregular migration via Canary Islands
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley de Extranjería regulates immigration for non-EU nationals. Spain has significant immigration (13%+ of residents are foreign-born). Major migrant communities: Latin American (privileged language/cultural ties), Moroccan, Romanian, Chinese. Spain provides a fast-track to citizenship (10 years residency, 2 years for Latin American nationals). The Canary Islands face severe pressure from Atlantic route migration from West Africa — arrivals exceeded 39,000 in 2023. Spain has EU-Africa migration agreements (Morocco, Mauritania, Senegal) to manage flows. Spain provides 'arraigo' (rootedness) regularization for undocumented migrants with 3+ years residence and social integration evidence — a relatively humane pathway used by thousands annually.
laws.penalty: Illegal stay: deportation, entry ban. False documentation: criminal prosecution. Employers of undocumented workers: fines €10,000 per worker.
exceptions: EU Blue Card available for highly skilled workers
Latin American nationals have bilateral treaty advantages
Child migrants (unaccompanied minors) have special protection and cannot be deported

quiz.q: What relatively humanitarian provision does Spain's immigration law include for long-term undocumented residents?
options: Arraigo (rootedness) regularization for undocumented migrants with 3+ years of residence and social integration evidence
Free healthcare regardless of legal status
quiz.explanation: Spain's 'arraigo' provisions allow undocumented migrants who have lived in Spain for 3+ years (arraigo social) to regularize their status by demonstrating social integration — language, community ties, employment history. This pragmatic approach acknowledges that long-term residents have built lives in Spain regardless of their initial entry status.

laws.title: Agencia Tributaria — Spanish Tax Authority and Fiscal Federalism
laws.subtitle: Spain's tax system and the complexity of regional fiscal arrangements
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Agencia Tributaria (AEAT) collects national taxes. Spain has a complex fiscal federalism: the Basque Country and Navarre have the 'Concierto/Convenio Económico' — they collect all taxes in their territory and transfer a fixed quota to the state, keeping the rest. All other autonomous communities receive transfers from the central government and have limited tax autonomy. This creates resentment from Catalonia (which claims it transfers more than it receives) and allegations of preferential treatment for the Basque Country. Spanish income tax is split state/regional (roughly 50/50). The wealth tax (Impuesto sobre el Patrimonio) — abolished in 2008, restored temporarily in 2011 — has been repeatedly contested by regions.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: penalties 50-150% of unpaid tax, interest. Criminal prosecution for evasion over €120,000. Serious non-compliance: up to 6 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Basque and Navarre fiscal autonomy under historical rights (fueros) is constitutionally protected
Canary Islands have special fiscal zone (ZEC) and reduced VAT (IGIC)
Ceuta and Melilla have zero VAT (IPSI)

quiz.q: What makes the Basque Country and Navarre's fiscal arrangement with Spain unique compared to all other regions?
options: They pay no taxes to the central government
They collect all taxes in their territory and transfer only a fixed quota (cupo) to the central state, keeping the rest
They receive double the EU structural funds
quiz.explanation: The Concierto Económico (Basque) and Convenio (Navarre) give these regions the right to collect all taxes within their territory and transfer only a negotiated 'cupo' (quota) to the central state. This is the inverse of the system for other regions, giving Basque Country and Navarre far greater fiscal independence — a right based on medieval fueros (regional laws) preserved in the 1978 Constitution.

laws.title: Ley de Costas — Spain's Coastal Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Strict rules protecting Spain's coastline from development
laws.fullDescription: Spain's Ley de Costas (1988, reformed 2013) declares Spain's entire coastline public property (dominio público marítimo-terrestre). The 'protection zone' extends 100 meters from the highest tide mark where no new construction is permitted; the 'influence zone' extends 500 meters with strong planning restrictions. Properties built before 1988 retain rights but face demolition when they expire. The law has resulted in controversial demolitions — including houses in Sancti-Petri (Cádiz) and Almería. Spain's coastline is heavily developed from 1960s-1980s tourism boom. Illegal buildings persist despite the law. The Catalan and Basque costs have additional regional protection. Climate change threatens coastal erosion particularly in the Cantabrian coast.
laws.penalty: Illegal coastal construction: demolition orders, fines. Development without environmental impact assessment: project suspension.
exceptions: Pre-1988 properties retain 'concesiones' (licenses) for a set period
Port infrastructure and approved coastal defense works are exempt
Aquaculture facilities have special authorization procedures
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica — Costas

quiz.q: Under Spain's Ley de Costas, what distance from the highest tide mark is subject to the strictest development prohibition?
quiz.explanation: Spain's Ley de Costas establishes a 'zona de protección' (protection zone) of 100 meters from the highest tide mark where no new construction is permitted. Beyond this, a 500-meter 'zona de influencia' has strong planning restrictions. Spain's entire coastline is declared public property (dominio público), meaning private permanent ownership of beach front is legally impossible.
